author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: RSF preps new front from Ethiopia, pummels Blue Nile; In Kordofan, RSF conducts ‘field’ executions, digs in heels at Nuhud; Dagris prison dispute stalls registry; Gov’t criticizes UN fact-finding renewal
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


With all eyes turned toward the escalating conflict in Ethiopia that is teetering on the brink of becoming a wider regional war, the Rapid Support Forces stepped up their attacks on the Sudan war’s southeastern front this week. 


Blue Nile’s

Wad al-Mahi

 locality in the east of the state bore the brunt of the escalation. The RSF launched an attack from Ethiopia on Saturday and seized the Kadalo mountains area, which sits near the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and Roseires Dam reservoir. This coincided with a drone campaign against Damazin, which included strikes on the homes of Blue Nile Governor Ahmed Badry and Regional Finance Minister Abbas Kara, fuel stations, military sites, universities and mosques. 


The military has hit back, launching airstrikes on RSF positions in

Wad al-Mahi and tried to reassure residents. As of Sunday, about

2,800 people are estimated to have been displaced from 10 villages in Wad al-Mahi.


But action in the southeastern front wasn’t limited to the Blue Nile. Large numbers of RSF fighters have been moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa in recent weeks in preparation to transfer them toward Sudan’s eastern border, where they are expected to gear up for an attack on the Fashaga border strip in Gadarif State, according to an RSF source and another source informed of the mobilization arrangements who spoke to Mada Masr. 


In anticipation of escalating attacks on the border, the Sudanese military has reinforced its positions in the east, military sources tell Mada Masr. And on Wednesday, military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visited the 11th Infantry Division in Khashm al-Gerba, Kassala State, which borders Gadarif to the north.


On the western front, the military is preparing to attack the remaining RSF-held areas in North Kordofan and advance into West Kordofan, with eyes set on Um Bader and Hamra al-Sheikh in northwestern North Kordofan. Meanwhile, the RSF is digging its heels in West Kordofan, with the group having dug trenches and built earth berms around the strategic city of Nuhud to guard against surprise attacks, an activist in the state told Mada Masr.


West Kordofan also saw yet another attack on an aid truck this week, with Khartoum laying blame for the strike at the feet of the RSF and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Abdel Aziz al-Hilu faction). 


In Um Bader, a social media video of the execution of 23 detainees is raising concern. While the RSF-led Tasis government tried to pin the executions on the military, three sources from the paramilitary group confirmed that the RSF had carried out the ‘field’ executions. As to why, the RSF sources’ accounts conflicted with those of medical sources and relatives of one of the men killed who spoke to Mada Masr.

But both Tasis and officials in Khartoum are keen to pursue justice, even if a Tasis official continued to dismiss the RSF’s implications when presented with what sources from the paramilitary told Mada Masr. 


In Darfur, the joint forces push toward Geneina continues to stall, with territory swapping hands. The US’s politicking over the Darfur arms embargo — which has done next to nothing to stop the flow of weapons through Darfur or seen the provider of those arms in the United Arab Emirates face international criticism — got kicked down the road for another two months, as DC continues its push to extend the embargo across the whole country. The UN’s fact-finding committee on Sudan did get its mandate renewed, much to the chagrin of the government in Khartoum, which sees any form of international intervention as an infringement on its sovereignty. And opacity around the infamous Dagris prison, where an estimated 20,000 people are being detained, has posed a roadblock in the government-RSF prisoner exchange registry process. 


In yet another senior defection from the paramilitary group, Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary, the commander of an RSF special operations group, announced on Thursday that he and around 300 officers and soldiers with 30 combat vehicles would join the military. You can read all about how the defections are symptomatic of a larger contradiction at the core of the RSF project in a Mada Masr investigation

published

earlier this week.

author: Marta Mboka Tveit
title: Utopia is not a metaphor
content:
The recent popularity of the term “Afrotopia” inspired me to revisit Thomas More’s original

Utopia

 (1516). Rereading the novel led me to rethink what we mean when we talk about ideology, future-casting, and visioning as praxis.

“Utopia” or “utopic” is today a widely used term across a variety of fields and contexts. People often use the term derogatorily, as a tired metaphor, carrying connotations of naiveté or veiled dystopian impulses. It gestures vaguely toward paradise, toward the promised land, but carries with it a whiff of the opposite. Don’t be naive, the contemporary connotation seems to say; don’t fall for the lies, don’t dream too big. Recently, daring scholarship has given the term a new, promised-land spin: for instance, in Felwine Sarr’s bold essay

Afrotopia

 (2020), a poetic call for an African utopian philosophy of self-reinvention for the 21st century, and, more recently, in Joseph Agbakoba and Marita Rainsborough’s

Beyond Decolonial African Philosophy

 (2025).

But reading

Utopia

, I was surprised by how concrete and policy-oriented the novel is. Its protagonist, Raphael Hythloday (sort of an early anthropologist), is in a debate with a fictionalized version of More himself and some others, and ends up talking about his visit to an island called Utopia, a visit that has profoundly changed him. Hythloday talks about how they organize life there, and how it’s going really well. In other words, the book is, thin veil of fiction aside, a set of policy recommendations. Utopia is an imagined place that has implemented these recommendations, which, as More understood them, result in a more egalitarian, life-supporting society. That’s all it is — no soaring, elusive nothing.

Thomas More (1478–1535) was a Renaissance man and deeply Catholic. An English lawyer, scholar, statesman, and writer, he entered royal service under King Henry VIII, eventually rising to the high office of Lord Chancellor in 1529. In 1516, when he wrote

Utopia

, he was living through the transition from the late medieval period to the early Renaissance, when society was rigidly hierarchical, dominated by the monarchy, the nobility, and the powerful Church. Corruption and the abuse of power were widespread among both political and religious leaders. More himself would pay for his convictions: in 1535 he was beheaded for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church in England.

Utopia

, it turns out, was not written as a metaphor for paradise, or some other magical place to house lofty dreams and impossible longings. It was written for those trying to organize. Like “utopia,” “democracy” or “the democratic society” has conventionally become a vague, transcendental thing, an ideal to be striven for but never reached, perhaps even unreachable. Yet early Athenian democracy was grounded in concrete institutional reforms rather than abstract ideals. In the early sixth century BCE, Solon’s reforms, widely understood as a foundational precursor to democracy, addressed both economic and political inequalities through specific measures: the

seisachtheia

, which canceled debt bondage; the establishment of legal recourse for broader segments of the citizen body; and the organization of political participation according to wealth classes, as Aristotle records in the

Constitution of the Athenians

.

The Athenians, we are told, would sweep a rope dipped in red dye through the crowds in the marketplace to herd people into the public meetings. That’s not mystic, timpani-and-marble, city-on-the-hill, shining-Athena stuff. That’s sandal prints in mud, overturned fruit stands, snotty crying children, slippery bodies slapped together — overcrowded, stinky, sweaty, loud democracy.

Perhaps there is something useful to be reminded of here in the current moment, which is calling for a radical reimagination of social order. Neither Athenian democracy nor More’s

Utopia

 was originally introduced as an ideal, a shining, vague star in the distance to reach toward. They were policy recommendations for the then and there, for a place and time, suited to fit a certain group. What would the equivalent place-and-time, tailor-fitted African societal epitomes look like?

Resetting the mechanisms of collective visioning requires, first of all, setting aside some of the major constraints of the present. Forget the debt for a minute. Leave the contract negotiation for tomorrow. Put that blaring traffic cone from across the Atlantic on mute. These …

author: Amy Goodman
title: Tens of Thousands Protest in India Against Modi Government’s Voter Roll Purges
content:
At least 7,000 people in New Delhi were detained on Saturday.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Tens of thousands of people in India have taken to the streets in recent days to protest the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls, a large majority of which are believed to be opposed to Narendra Modi’s ruling BJP party. The demonstrations, joined by leaders from India’s opposition parties, are being led by students and the youth-led “Cockroach” movement. Tens of thousands of security forces, including paramilitary and police, were out on the streets over the weekend cracking down on the uprising, detaining protesters en masse, including lawyers, journalists and protest leaders.

The demonstrations “represent an outpouring of anger, of frustration at what many Indians feel is the fact that their democracy has been taken away,” says Shoaib Daniyal, political editor of Scroll, who was arrested on Saturday along with 7,000 other protesters. He points out that “the deletions have affected Muslims far more than they have affected other Indians.”

On Monday, in one of largest recent protests in India’s capital of New Delhi, India’s main opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi of the Congress Party, led a march to the Supreme Court of India. “This march has become a people’s march, with all of them heading towards this constitutional authority, which they feel should safeguard the rights of Indian people, especially this very basic right to vote,” says Jahnavi Sen, managing editor of The Wire.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

ANJALI KAMAT: In India, the right-wing government of Narendra Modi is facing its biggest challenge yet in 12 years in power, as tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets to protest what they call vote theft. At issue is the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls, and the vast majority of those deletions are believed to be opposed to Prime Minister Modi’s ruling BJP party.

The protests are being led by students and the youth Cockroach movement and joined by leaders from the opposition parties. They’re demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and an overhaul of the electoral system. The Cockroach movement started after the chief justice of India’s Supreme Court compared unemployed youth to cockroaches earlier this year.

Today, in one of largest recent protests in India’s capital of New Delhi, India’s main opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi of the Congress Party, is leading a march to the Supreme Court of India. Speaking to reporters earlier today, Gandhi reiterated the call for the election commissioner to resign.

RAHUL GANDHI: Narendra Modi is blocking the whole town, is putting 30,000-40,000 police people outside. For what? Because the opposition is asking one question: Prove to us that you have not cheated in the election. Prove to us that you’ve not cheated in the election.

AMY GOODMAN: The Modi government put New Delhi in lockdown ahead of Saturday’s protests, canceling trains to the city, shutting down metro stations, even suspending mobile internet in large parts of Delhi. Tens of thousands of security forces, including paramilitary and police, were mobilized across the city, and at least 7,000 people were detained Saturday alone, including protest leaders, lawyers and journalists. This is a protester speaking to reporters from inside a van where he was detained.

PROTESTER: [translated] The Modi government is scared of us. That is why we have been picked up from halfway. We didn’t even know where they were trying to bring us. [in English] This is just fear. And they are afraid of us because they have done something wrong, and you cannot do something wrong with the people of this country, man.

AMY GOODMAN: Several Cockroach movement leaders were also arrested right off the plane as they arrived in Delhi for the protest Saturday morning. After being released the next morning, Saurav Das, one of the leaders of the Cockroach People’s Party, vowed protests would continue.

SAURAV DAS: The protests are on. The protests will go on. [translated] The youth of the country have woken up. The youth of the country are asking for accountability. The peaceful protests will go on until they fix accountability. And now the protests will not only happen in Delhi, but in the whole country.

author: Andrea
title: ᑰᔾᔪᐊᕐᒥ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖓᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑏᑦ ᓅᑕᐅᕗᑦ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐋᓪᒧᑦ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see

Tusaajiapik elders home residents being relocated to Montreal

.


ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᑰᔾᔪᐊᑉ ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᒃ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖓᓂ ᓅᑕᐅᕗᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᖁᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐋᓪ ᓯᓚᑎᑦᑎᐊᖓᓂ 1,500 ᑭᓛᒥᑐᓄᑦ ᓂᒋᕐᒧᑦ.


ᓅᑕᐅᓂᖓ, ᑭᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᔭᕆᑐᔪᓄᑦ ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑕᐅᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᒥ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᒥ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 30−ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑎᓕᐅᖅᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᓕᐊᕆ ᐅᐊᑦᒧᑦ, ᐅᖓᕙ ᑐᓚᑦᑕᕕᒃ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᕕᖓᓂ ᐃᓱᒻᒥᖅᑐᐃᔨᖓᓂ; ᐊᒻᒪᔭᓇᕗ ᒥᐅᓂᒃ−ᐅᐊᑦᑭᓐᔅ, ᓄᓇᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐃᓱᒻᒥᖅᑐᐃᔨᖓᓐᓂ.


“ᓅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᓯᒪᕗᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᔪᓯᓂᐊᖅᐳᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᓅᑕᐅᕌᓂᒃᐸᑕ,” ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖅ ᐅᖃᖅᓯᒪᕗᖅ.


ᓅᑕᐅᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᐱᖓᓱᐃᓕᖓᔪᒥ ᐊᖏᕈᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᒥᔪᒥᒃ Argyle Inc.−ᑯᑦ ᐊᑯᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐸᖅᑭᕝᕕᐅᔪᒥ, ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᐅᔪᒥ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐋᓪ ᓯᓚᑎᑦᑎᐊᖓᓂ ᐳᐊᐃᓐᑦ ᑭᓕᐊᕐᒥ.


“ᐊᖏᕈᑎ ᑐᕌᕋᓱᐊᖅᐳᖅ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ, ᐸᖅᑭᑦᑎᐊᖅᑐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᒧᑦ ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓂᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐆᒪᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᕙᑎᐅᔪᒥ, ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᓛᓐᓂᓚᐅᓱᖓᕐᒥ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖅᑯᓯᑐᖃᖅᑎᒍᑦ ᓂᕿᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᐅᔪᓂ,” ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᑲᔪᓯᕗᖅ.


ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓅᑕᐅᒍᑎᒃ, ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᒃ ᒪᑐᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ.


ᐅᐊᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᐅᓂᒃ-ᐅᐊᑦᑭᓐᔅ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᖅᓯᒪᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 1−ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐅᕈᓐᓇᙱᖦᖢᑎᒃ, ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᖓᑕ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᓂ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ.


ᑰᔾᔪᐊᕐᒥ, ᓯᕗᓪᓕᐅᔪᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᕗᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᕋᔭᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᖏᓂᖓᓂ ᑎᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᖕᒥ ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᒐᒃᓴᐃᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᖓᓐᓄᑦ, ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖅ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ. ᐊᑭᖓᓂ ᓇᓚᐅᑦᑖᕆᔭᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᓂᕆᐅᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᖃᖓᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅ ᑕᒪᑐᒪᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖑᔪᒥ.


ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᒃ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ “ᐱᔭᕆᑐᔪᓂ” ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑕᐅᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᑉ ᐅᖅᑰᓴᐅᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᒥ, ᐱᑎᑦᑎᔪᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᕿᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓅᑕᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓂᕆᐅᒐᒃᓴᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᐃᑉᕆᓕᒥ 13−ᓄᑦ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ, 10−ᖑᔪᑦ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᕆᔭᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ ᑕᐃᔅᓱᒪᓂ ᑲᐃᓪᓗᐊᕈᑎᓃᑦᑐᓂ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᐃᒡᓕᖕᒦᖏᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ.


ᐅᐱᕐᙶᖑᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ, ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ 35−ᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᓂ, ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᓗᐊᖅᓴᐃᔨᓂᑦ, ᐃᓄᓕᕆᔨᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖅ ᐸᖅᑭᔨᐅᔪᓂᑦ.

author: William Gillis
title: အနာခီဝါဒ၏ ထူးခြားသော အစွန်းရောက်ဆန်းသစ်မှု
content:
William


Gillis

. Original:

The Distinct Radicalism of Anarchism

, December 24

th

, 2016. Translated into Burmese by Hein Htet Kyaw.


အနာခီဝါဒသမားတွေဟာ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမားတွေနဲ့ အဓိကကွဲပြားချက်ကို အစွန်းရောက်မှု သို့မဟုတ် အမြစ်တွယ်မှု အနိမ့်အမြင့်အဆင့်နဲ့ပဲ တိုင်းတာပြလေ့ရှိကြတယ်။ ဒါကို အသုံးများတဲ့ အသုံးအနှုန်းနဲ့ ပြောရရင် မာက်စ်ဝါဒက “နိုင်ငံရေး” ကို ဦးတည်ပြီး၊ ငါတို့ (အနာခီဝါဒ) ကတော့ “ကျင့်ဝတ်ဆိုင်ရာ” ကို ဦးတည်တာ ဖြစ်တယ်။


ဒီလို ခွဲခြားသတ်မှတ်မှုကို အသိအမှတ်ပြုလိုက်ပြီဆိုတာနဲ့ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမားရော အနာခီဝါဒသမားပါ ဝမ်းသာအားရ လက်ခံကြတာများတယ်။ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမားတွေ ပျော်သွားရတဲ့အကြောင်းကတော့ သူတို့ကိုယ်သူတို့ “လက်တွေ့ကျသူတွေ” ဆိုတဲ့ ပုံစံထဲ အံဝင်ခွင်ကျ ဖြစ်သွားလို့ပဲ။ ဒါ့အပြင် မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမား အများစုဟာ ကျင့်ဝတ်တရား မရှိသူတွေ ဖြစ်ကြပြီး ကျင့်ဝတ်ဆိုင်ရာ တတ်သိပညာရပ်တွေကို စုံစမ်းလေ့လာနေဖို့ အကြောင်းမရှိဘူးလို့ ထင်ကြတယ်။ သူတို့ဆီမှာ ရှိပြီးသား သို့မဟုတ် ငြင်းခုံစရာမလိုဘဲ ထင်ရှားနေတဲ့ ဆန္ဒတွေကိုပဲ အကောင်အထည်ဖော်ဖို့ စိတ်ဝင်စားကြပြီး ဘာတန်ဖိုးတွေ၊ ဘာဆန္ဒတွေကို ဆုပ်ကိုင်ရမလဲဆိုတာ စိစစ်ဖို့ စိတ်မဝင်စားကြဘူး။ ကျင့်ဝတ်ဆိုင်ရာ တတ်သိပညာကို တန်ဖိုးထားပါတယ်ဆိုတဲ့ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမား အနည်းငယ်ကလည်း အဲဒါကို စနစ်တကျ လေ့လာဖို့ ငြင်းဆန်ကြသလို၊ သူတို့ရဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေးလုပ်ငန်းတွေနဲ့လည်း ခွဲခြားထားတတ်ကြတယ်။ တစ်ခါတစ်ရံ ကျင့်ဝတ်ကို စဉ်းစားမိရင်လည်း အနာခီဝါဒသမားတွေနဲ့ အရမ်းနီးစပ်တဲ့ သဘောထားမျိုး ဖြစ်သွားလေ့ရှိတယ်။


အခြားတစ်ဖက်မှာတော့ အနာခီဝါဒသမားတွေက ဒီလိုခွဲခြားမှုကို သဘောကျကြတယ်၊ အကြောင်းကတော့ ဒါဟာ အစွန်းရောက်ဆန်းသစ်မှုရဲ့ ကွဲပြားချက် မလွဲမသွေ ဖြစ်နေလို့ပဲ။ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမားတွေ အမြဲပြောလေ့ရှိတဲ့ Super-structures ဆိုတာဟာ ပိုမိုရှုပ်ထွေးပြီး တက်ကြွလှုပ်ရှားနေတဲ့ လက်တွေ့ဘဝရဲ့ အထက်မှာ ပေါ်လွင်နေတဲ့ ရိုးရှင်းတဲ့ ရုပ်ကြမ်း အယူအဆတွေပဲ ဖြစ်တယ်။ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမားက “လူတန်းစား” ဆိုတဲ့ ခေါင်းစဉ်နဲ့ စကားပြောရတာကြိုက်ပြီး၊ အနာခီဝါဒသမားကတော့ “လူတစ်ဦးချင်းစီ၏ ဆက်ဆံရေးနှင့် ထိတွေ့ဆက်ဆံမှုများ” ကို ပဓာနထား ပြောဆိုကြတယ်။ ဒီသဘောနဲ့ဆိုရင် ငါတို့ အနာခီဝါဒသမားတွေဟာ ပိုမိုစကြာဝဠာဆန်သလို၊ ပိုပြီးတော့လည်း အသေးစိတ်ကျတယ်။ သမိုင်းကြောင်းရဲ့ သီးခြားဖြစ်ရပ်တွေအပေါ် မှီခိုမှုနည်းတဲ့ ပိုမိုအခြေခံကျတဲ့ ရွေ့လျားမှုတွေကို ငါတို့ ရှာဖွေကြတယ်၊ အဲဒီလို ရှာဖွေခြင်းအားဖြင့် သီးခြားအခြေအနေတွေကို ပိုမိုအသေးစိတ်ကျကျ လေ့လာဆန်းစစ်နိုင်တဲ့ နည်းလမ်းတွေကို ရရှိလာတယ်။ ဖိနှိပ်သူနဲ့ အဖိနှိပ်ခံ လူတန်းစားဆိုတဲ့ ရှုထောင့်ကနေ လေ့လာဆန်းစစ်တာဟာ အသုံးဝင်မှုရှိတယ်ဆိုတာကို လက်ခံပေမဲ့၊ အဲဒီလို ခေါင်းစဉ်တပ်တာတွေရဲ့ မရေရာမှုကို မြင်နိုင်ပြီး အဲဒီထက် ပိုမိုနက်ရှိုင်းတဲ့ နည်းလမ်းတွေကို အသုံးပြုဖို့ ဝမ်းမြောက်စွာ ဆောင်ရွက်ကြတယ်။ အစွန်းရောက်တဲ့ ရပ်တည်ချက်ဆိုတာဟာ ရုပ်ကြမ်းအဆင့်မှာရှိတဲ့ ယေဘုယျကောက်ချက်တွေရဲ့ အသိအမြင်ကို ထိန်းသိမ်းထားရင်း၊ အဲဒါတွေဟာ အခြေခံအကျဆုံး မဟုတ်ဘဲ အဏုမြူအဆင့်မှာရှိတဲ့ ပိုမိုနက်ရှိုင်းတဲ့ ရွေ့လျားမှုတွေနဲ့ အစားထိုးနိုင်တယ်ဆိုတာကို နားလည်တာ ဖြစ်တယ်။


မာက်စ်ဝါဒဟာ “အင်ဂျင်နီယာဘာသာရပ်” နဲ့ တူနေရင်၊ အနာခီဝါဒဟာ “ရူပဗေဒ” နဲ့ အလွန်တူပါတယ်။ ရူပဗေဒရဲ့ ရှုထောင့်ဟာ အင်ဂျင်နီယာရဲ့ “ရိုးရိုးလက်တွေ့ကျမှု” ကို အနိုင်ရသွားတယ်လို့ ငါယူဆတာဟာ ဆန်းကြယ်တဲ့ကိစ္စ မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။ မာက်စ်ဝါဒသမားတွေက “ရိုးရိုးလက်တွေ့ကျမှု” ကို အကောင်းဆုံး စတင်ရာအဖြစ် မြင်ကြတာလည်း မဆန်းပါဘူး။ မင်းသိပြီးသားအရာနဲ့ စတင်ပြီး၊ အဲဒါ ပျက်စီးသွားတဲ့အခါ သို့မဟုတ် မဖြစ်မနေ ပြောင်းလဲရတော့မယ့် အခြေအနေရောက်မှသာ မော်ဒယ်ကို မွမ်းမံကြတယ်။ ဒါဟာ မာက်စ်ဝါဒ စကားဝိုင်းတွေမှာ အလုပ်သမားနဲ့အရင်းရှင်တိုက်ပွဲထက် ကျော်လွန်တဲ့ အရာတွေကို မော်ဂျူးစနစ်လို ဖြည့်စွက်စဉ်းစားလာရတဲ့ အကြောင်းရင်းပဲ။ လွတ်မြောက်ရေးနဲ့ ဖိနှိပ်ရေးဆိုင်ရာ စကားဝိုင်းအသစ်တွေဟာ (ရိုးရှင်းတဲ့ လူတန်းစား ပဋိပက္ခပုံပြင်တွေအဖြစ် စာရင်းသွင်းခံရပြီး) မာက်စ်ဝါဒ အတွေးအခေါ်ထဲကို မသပ်မရပ် တွဲဆက်ခံရကာ တစ်ခုလုံး ဒေါင်ဒေါင်မြည်အောင် မောင်းနှင်နေရတယ်။


ယခုအခါ မကောင်းတဲ့ သဘောနဲ့ “ဝိသေသ စိစစ်ခွဲခြားရေး နိုင်ငံရေး” လို့ ခေါ်ဆိုနေကြတာဟာ များသောအားဖြင့် ဒီလိုမျိုး ရိုးရှင်းတဲ့ သဘောတရား ရေးဆွဲမှုရဲ့ ဆက်လက်ဖြစ်ပေါ်နေမှုပဲ ဖြစ်ပါတယ်။ ခေတ်သစ် လူမှုရေးတရားမျှတမှုဟာ အစွန်းရောက် အနည်းငယ်ရဲ့ စကားဝိုင်းကနေ လူသန်းပေါင်းများစွာဆီ မြန်မြန်ဆန်ဆန် ရောက်ရှိသွားတဲ့ လွတ်မြောက်ရေး အသိအမြင်တွေရဲ့ ရလဒ် ဖြစ်တယ်။ အသစ်အဆန်းတွေကို ရုတ်တရက် ရင်ဆိုင်လိုက်ရတဲ့အခါ အချို့သော ချုံ့ယူမှု သို့မဟုတ် ရိုးရှင်းအောင် လုပ်ဆောင်မှုတွေ ဖြစ်ပေါ်လာတာ သဘာဝပါပဲ။


ထို့ကြောင့် လူမှုရေးတရားမျှတမှုဟာ  ယေဘုယျအားဖြင့် ကျင့်ဝတ် သို့မဟုတ် ဥပဒေစနစ်တစ်ခု (အစိုးရ အကြမ်းဖက်မှုထက် ဂုဏ်သိက္ခာဖြင့် ထိန်းချုပ်ထားသော ဗဟိုမဲ့စနစ်) ကို ဖန်တီးဖို့ လက်တွေ့ကျကျ ကြိုးပမ်းမှုတစ်ခု ဖြစ်လာခဲ့တယ်။ ဒါဟာ ကျင့်ဝတ်စနစ်နဲ့ လုံးဝကွဲပြားတဲ့ လုပ်ဆောင်ချက် ဖြစ်ပါတယ်။ စိစစ်ခွဲခြားရေး လူမှုရေးတရားမျှတမှုရဲ့ အကြီးမားဆုံး အားသာချက်နဲ့ အားနည်းချက်ကတော့ အကြောင်းရင်းအပေါ် မှီခိုမှုမရှိအောင် ကြိုးစားထားတာပဲ ဖြစ်တယ်။ ဥပမာ – အမျိုးသမီးမုန်းတီးမှုကို ဘာကြောင့် ဆန့်ကျင်ရသလဲဆိုတာ စိစစ်ဖို့ မကြိုးစားပါဘူး။ နားထောင်သူတွေဟာ အတူတူဘဲ တန်ဖိုးထားကြတယ်လို့ ယူဆလိုက်တယ် (သို့မဟုတ်) လူတွေရဲ့ အခံတန်ဖိုးတွေနဲ့ မသက်ဆိုင်ဘဲ လူမှုယဉ်ကျေးမှု …

author: Jeremy Appel, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous rights at forefront of anti-AI data centre rally in ‘Edmonton’
content:
Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation speaks at an Oct. 3 rally against data centres outside the ‘Alberta’ legislature building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton).

Photo by Jeremy Appel


This story was originally published in

Alberta Native News

 on Oct. 6,

and appears here with permission and style edits

,

with added context from the author’s

earlier article

 from May 14

.


More than 100 people gathered outside the Legislative Assembly building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton) on Oct. 3 to protest the provincial and federal governments’ permissive approach towards building artificial intelligence data centres.  


Elder Taz Bouchier opened the rally with a land acknowledgement before tying the proposed 7.5-gigawatt Wonder Valley data centre near Grande Prairie’s potential water usage to the oil industry’s plans to release treated tailings fluids into the Athabasca watershed. 


“When did people lose sight of how valuable water is to living? When money came into play. That’s all these data centers are about,” said Bouchier. 


Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is challenging the province’s decision to award a water license of 24-million cubic metres to the Municipal District of Greenview for Wonder Valley without consulting the Treaty 8 First Nation, which relies on the Smoky River for its water. 


At the protest, Chief Sheldon Sunshine outlined a series of “very basic questions” he has for data centre proponents, including whether existing rules are sufficient “for the size and scale of what is being proposed” and whether there are sufficient water protections.


READ MORE:


AI data centers are booming. Indigenous People want help protecting their lands and knowledge


“What happens to our communities when these projects operate for decades?” Sunshine asked. “What happens to the land? What happens to the water? What happens to the wildlife? What happens to the air quality? What happens when multiple projects are operating in the same region? And perhaps most importantly, where is the assessment of the cumulative impacts?


“We can’t look at every project at one time and pretend the others don’t exist. We have to look at the whole picture.”


As first

reported

 by online news outlet

Canada’s National Observer

, Environment Alberta has exempted Wonder Valley from an environmental assessment. 


“Why are governments creating pathways to accelerate these developments before the public has confidence that the rules are strong enough? Why is the push happening so fast? What concessions are being made to attract these projects? Who negotiated those concessions?” asked Chief Sunshine. 


“Those are reasonable questions. Asking them does not make us anti-development. It makes us responsible.” 


He emphasized that he understands the government’s “economic strategy behind these projects,” in terms of attempting to create a new market for the province’s substantial natural gas resources. 


“But economic development cannot come at any cost,” said Sunshine. “You cannot build a new economy by putting the foundation of that economy on water that communities depend on, land that cannot be replaced, or an electrical system that people already rely on.


“You cannot call something responsible development simply because it creates jobs. Responsible development means understanding the consequences before you build.”


Edmonton-Strathcona NDP MP Heather McPherson opened her remarks by “acknowledging that Indigenous people in this country are on the front lines of this fight, and on the front lines of so many fights that we are being asked to fight as citizens right now,” referring to First Nations’

opposition

 to the province’s separatist movement. 


“We all owe Indigenous people in this province a debt of gratitude,” she added, “for being on the front line, protecting our sovereignty, protecting our climate, protecting our water and our land.”


READ MORE:


After court win, First Nations denounce ‘Alberta’ premier’s separation referendum plan


McPherson called it greatly “frustrating” that data centres are being fast-tracked while crucial community needs are being unmet. 


“We can’t build the homes that people need in this community, but we can build a data centre,” she said. “We can’t build clean water facilities for people in this country, but we can build a data center.


“The priority here for this government is to make billionaires wealthy at the expense of every single one of us here.”

title: White Nationalists Off Secwépemc Territory
content:
There is a growing white supremacist genocide denial movement in so-called Canada.

On September 27th members of the Second Sons, a white nationalist militia, marched on unceded Secwépemc territory carrying racist banners near a former residential school where mass graves of Indigenous children were discovered.

This action was timed to occur three days before National Truth and Reconciliation Day a flawed and limited attempt to acknowledge Canada’s genocide of Indigenous peoples.

The Second Sons are tightly connected to the so-called ‘Active Clubs’ movement and have called to remove non-white people from Canada at gunpoint.

The Secwépemc have a long history of resistance to Canadian colonialism, including the Gustaffson Lake standoff in 1995, and more recently, the Tiny House Warrior movement, launched in resistance to the TransMountain Pipeline project.

White supremacy is inherent to settler colonialism.

Settler anarchists have a special responsibility to support Indigenous sovereignty and confront white nationalists wherever they rear their ugly heads.

Get together. Crew up. Confront white supremacy in all its forms.

author: Maya Schenwar
title: We Must Move Beyond the Era of State-Sponsored, State-Celebrated Murder
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


  Christa Pike woke up on October 6 in a Tennessee hospital with a blood clot and pneumonia, handcuffed and shackled to her bed, having become the first known person to survive an execution via lethal injection. On September 30, the state of Tennessee tried to murder Pike. Instead, it put her through an hour and a half of difficulty breathing as she intermittently gasped for air and was eventually sent into critical condition, in a notoriously “botched execution” — in other words,

torture

. As Sandra Babcock, one of Pike’s attorneys,

put it

 on

Democracy Now

: “Christa Pike … has just experienced the most agonizing attempt at lethal injection in the country’s history.”


  Conversations in the wake of this torture have, understandably, focused on the exceptional circumstances of the attempted killing. However, this is also an important moment to recognize the depths of brutality in which this country wallows, such that the killing of a person by their own government only tends to make front page news when it is “botched.” It is also a key time to push ourselves to imagine beyond that violence, and to ask: What kind of world can we build, in which an execution is unthinkable?


  First, we must contend with the extent of our status-quo brutality. This vicious, not-so-new normal is illustrated by the fact that in the end, Pike’s attorneys, who fought persistently for her sentence to be commuted, were forced to argue for her to be

hanged

, as Pike rightly predicted that her small veins would make lethal injection a long and terrifyingly painful process. Let that sink in: We live in a country where mercy is a

hanging.


  Death penalty proponents have responded to Pike’s survival by advocating even harsher methods. U.S. Senator and Tennessee gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn responded, “The answer is simple: Bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly.” (Multiple state supreme courts have ruled the electric chair to be cruel and unusual punishment, citing examples like

six-inch flames

 erupting from the head of an electrocution victim.)


Tennessee State House Speaker Cameron Sexton

said

, “I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.” And in a cameo that should shock no one, Former Deputy Assistant Attorney John Yoo, infamous for authoring the

Torture Memos,


said

 on

Fox News

, “Tennessee is trying to use what is considered the most humane method of capital punishment, which is lethal injection. The court has allowed, and Tennessee could use, far more … hurtful, you know, methods like firing squad.”


  These pro-cruelty statements mark a chilling counter-trend regarding the death penalty. Throughout the early 21

st

 century, thanks to the efforts of an enduring anti-death penalty movement, executions significantly declined, pharmaceutical companies fled the execution-drug market, and medical professionals overwhelmingly refused to participate in executions.


  These shifts, of course, never went far enough, and states’ insistence that the alternative must be a lifelong prison sentence — death by incarceration, as dedicated organizers have termed it — has ingrained the use of endless punishment, marking another uphill battle.


This week, Trump approved the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years, and the Pentagon plans to livestream it.


  Yet even these changes are on thin ice. The last two years have witnessed a pronounced resurgence of executions. In the U.S., more people were killed by the state in 2025 than in any year since 2009. And by July of this year, Trump had already

begun

 more capital prosecutions than he’d launched in his whole first term in office. This week, Trump approved the

first U.S. military execution

 in more than 60 years, and the Pentagon plans to

livestream it

.

Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up

executive order

, which claimed that “only capital punishment can bring justice and restore order” in relation to “the vilest crimes.” In a memo in April of this year, Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) called on Congress to

broaden and accelerate

 use of the federal death penalty. And in a

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

Morland encouraged fellow journalists to preserve their own work rather than discard it, explaining that materials that may seem unremarkable today can become valuable historical records. The archives offer researchers an opportunity to explore the experiences and contributions of women journalists and document the development of organizations such as JAWS.

The reception highlighted the importance of preserving women’s experiences in journalism, particularly as the profession continues to confront challenges. JAWS is helping ensure the future generations can study their work and understand the history of feminist media.

As Ms. approaches its 55th anniversary in December, marking 25 years with the Feminist Majority Foundation as publisher, the gathering celebrated the relationships, reporting and feminist organizing that have sustained the magazine and the broader movement. Speakers closed by celebrating Ms., Gloria Steinem, and the community of women journalists whose work continues to shape feminist media.

author: Alison Avigayil Ramer
title: After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces
content:
This article

After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Since the massacres on Oct. 7, now three years ago, the news has brought a steady stream of horror and broken promises. The ceasefire in Gaza has been broken thousands of times; the ceasefire with Iran only holds until the next strike. Many of us have responded by going numb or turning away. Over these three years, I’ve come to believe that collective mourning can help movements build sturdier organizing infrastructure, move through paralysis and numbness, and get back to the long-term work of creating systemic change.


I’ve spent nearly two decades living and working as a human rights defender, mostly in Palestine and Israel. For years, I responded to atrocities the way much of the dominant organizing culture did at the time: strategically. I prepared statements, launched campaigns and mobilized our base. I worked through several wars and the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide. Even though my colleagues and I were often physically together, we rarely had the opportunity to collectively mourn. In fact, mourning was often seen as something only the privileged could afford. As organizers and solidarity activists, we were the ones who needed to push past the pain and keep mobilizing.


And then, after each war, large swaths of colleagues and organizers would burn out, and our movement would suffer a setback. Movement researchers Paul Gorski and Cher Chen, studying U.S. human rights and social justice activists, found that an estimated 50 to 60 percent of organizers eventually walk away from movement work and never return, burned out by a culture that treats overwork and self-sacrifice as necessary. That culture also leaves no room to mourn and process the secondary trauma that accumulates, hastening burnout. These kinds of cycles make it especially hard for movements seeking systemic change to sustain themselves.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


When Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023 and I was waiting in anticipation of the retaliation against Gaza, I knew I couldn’t respond with the same kind of organizing strategy that we usually use: preparation of advocacy statements, social media campaigns and fundraising appeals. I knew that while some people should and would continue that work, there also needed to be spaces for organizers and our base to mourn. And so, on Oct. 8, I opened a space for collective mourning online, sharing it in the many community, political and religious groups I was a part of, for anyone who needed somewhere to process what they were witnessing and feeling. Dozens of people joined: primarily my Jewish community at first, and then people from many faiths and chapters of my life, from Palestine to Palo Alto. 


As the assault on Gaza and the genocide continued, the room stayed open. More colleagues, including community organizers, artists, chaplains and psychologists, joined me in facilitating, and we held space for hundreds of people from across our communities to mourn together. We formed a collective called the

Social Change Sanctuary

 and developed a format that included facilitation and participation from attendees. Over time, we were invited to hold spaces for other communities in mourning. We’ve held spaces to grieve the ongoing genocide; climate catastrophes like the fires in Los Angeles; ICE raids, arrests and murders; and the war on Iran.


The Social Change Sanctuary hosts an Interdependence Day circle in 2025. (Alison Avigayil Ramer)


Participants repeatedly shared the difference it made in their lives to know they had a consistent space to mourn.


“In daily life, when something hurts, I turn away, I distract myself,” one participant told us. “But the collective mourning practice helped me move through the frozenness that constant news induced — helped me stop doomscrolling — and I’m able to return to my work.”


That participant went on to organize her community and raised $20,000 for refugees in Gaza. 


Another participant returned to their role as a chaplain, and extended her work to include “movement chaplaincy” holding one-on-one spaces for people doing solidarity work. 


Many participants also shared how witnessing the news with others enabled them to feel the emotions provoked by the headlines, leaving them feeling less isolated and more connected. That is co-regulation happening at …

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas.


Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by


nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?


AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.  


When you meet someone with a workplace or tenant issue, the whole solidarity network takes on the demands of the case, with those with the grievance–the issue(s) they want to fight around that directly affects them–being core organizers of their own campaign. We use direct action tactics, which means we don’t go through the courts or ask the cops or nonprofits to take care of the situation for us; we rely on just us to get the demand met by putting pressure on the boss or landlord until it becomes so unbearable they have no choice but to give in.


Like most solidarity networks there is a small group of core organizers who respond to the day- to-day needs of the organization. The people with the demands must be a part of this group. Then, there is a larger membership which is involved in many of the functions of the organization, but not all of its functions. They may pass out flyers with us, make phone calls, or research campaign targets, for example. Then there is a much larger network of people who will come out to actions when called on.


BRRN: Walk us through how you started it. Why this kind of organization, and what kinds of fights do you take on?


AK:

 Our specific solidarity network wanted to take on wage theft campaigns as our main, but not exclusive, area of struggle. We began working with another organization here that works in immigrant communities around stopping deportations. They were getting a lot of calls about wage theft, and helped us start the solidarity network to meet this need. Most of our initial calls came directly from them, and our first campaign came out of one of these calls. We also understand that the immigrant community, especially here in Texas, is very vulnerable to wage theft, and they often feel they do not have a lot of options for getting back stolen wages. We want to change that! Eventually, we want to create a citywide network of people who can respond to wage theft grievances, and other workplace and housing issues. We want to make bosses and landlords scared to even think about messing with us! 


In ATX, we have a small and unorganized left with a larger activist scene. A solidarity network is one form of organization that can work well under these conditions because you really only need a handful of core organizers and access to lots of people to show up to actions. We also see this form of organization being one in which committed leftists can develop relationships with other members of the working class. We see a lot of the left in ATX being very insular and removed from other everyday people. We feel it is important to be organizing in working-class communities since it is us as a class that are capable of transforming society. 


We also want to help normalize direct action tactics to push our collective ability to struggle even further. Ultimately, we would like to see more working-class organizations in our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and more. The solidarity network isn’t meant to be

the form

 of organization for widespread worker rebellion, but it is one form of organization that can respond to specific conditions that …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. It is just fascinating to me that despite the fact that she has been in folklore for centuries, no new media has come out about her in years, and now these two instances pop up in the same year. Three, if you count the experimental film Báthory by Carlos Atanes. Something seems to be in the (bloody) water.

Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps The Blood Countess isn’t quite as gay as it could be. Then again, apparently Ottinger wrote the screenplay in 1998, almost 30 years ago, so that could potentially account for that. But still, I won’t say no to a lesbian vampire film so I’ll probably still check it out when it makes its North American theatrical release in spring 2027.

author: Alfredo Seguel
title: Chile: Alertan que las nuevas Reglas del Uso de la Fuerza “no cumplen estándares de derechos humanos” y advierte “margen excesivo”
content:
Amnistía Internacional Chile advirtió que las Reglas del Uso de la Fuerza (RUF), aprobadas el 7 de octubre tras la muerte de dos policías, no cumplen estándares internacionales de derechos humanos. Su director, Rodrigo Bustos Bottai, criticó la ausencia de proporcionalidad, rendición de cuentas y prohibiciones esenciales, advirtiendo un mayor riesgo de abusos, especialmente en manifestaciones.


“Dejan a la ciudadanía en mayor desprotección”: Amnistía cuestiona la RUF aprobada  y advierte un “margen excesivo”


El reciente fallecimiento de dos policías aceleró la aprobación del proyecto de ley sobre las Reglas del Uso de la Fuerza (RUF) que llevaba en tramitación desde hace más de tres años.

 El 7 de octubre,  el texto fue aprobado por la Cámara de Diputados y Diputadas y posteriormente por el Senado. Al respecto, Rodrigo Bustos Bottai, director ejecutivo de Amnistía Internacional Chile, ha dicho:

“Las reglas tal como han sido aprobadas no cumplen con los estándares internacionales de derechos humanos.

Es preocupante que no contemplen adecuadamente principios fundamentales como la proporcionalidad y la rendición de cuentas, y que se hayan debilitado referencias esenciales a la prohibición de la tortura y de protección de grupos de especial protección como niñas, niños y adolescentes. Estas deficiencias abren la puerta a que puedan repetirse graves violaciones de derechos humanos, otorgando un margen excesivo de actuación a las policías y las Fuerzas Armadas y dejando a la ciudadanía en una situación de mayor desprotección

”.


Las Reglas del Uso de la Fuerza establecen las condiciones y límites bajo los cuales las policías y las Fuerzas Armadas pueden ejercer sus funciones

. El proyecto de ley busca entregar un marco común para determinar cuándo, cómo y con qué intensidad puede utilizarse la fuerza, así como establecer deberes y responsabilidades asociados a su empleo.


El Estado tiene la facultad de utilizar legítimamente la fuerza para proteger a las personas y mantener el orden público. Sin embargo, esta facultad debe ejercerse dentro de límites estrictos y de acuerdo con las obligaciones internacionales de derechos humanos.


Chile, como Estado parte de la Convención Americana sobre Derechos Humanos y del Pacto Internacional de Derechos Civiles y Políticos, está obligado a respetar y garantizar, entre otros, los derechos a la vida e integridad personal. Estos tratados se complementan con estándares específicos de Naciones Unidas sobre el uso de la fuerza y las armas de fuego, así como con la jurisprudencia de la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos.


Una regulación adecuada debe establecer, entre otros elementos, los principios de legalidad, necesidad, proporcionalidad y responsabilidad. Esto significa que la fuerza debe perseguir un objetivo legítimo, utilizarse solo cuando sea necesaria y recurrir a medios e intensidad acordes con la amenaza o resistencia enfrentada.


“Durante el estallido social pudimos ver las graves consecuencias del uso desproporcionado y abusivo de la fuerza, que dejó a miles de personas heridas y con lesiones de por vida. En ese momento, recomendamos con urgencia establecer reglas y protocolos más precisos y acordes con el derecho internacional. Sin embargo, esto aún no se ha cumplido, lo que abre la puerta, especialmente en contextos de manifestación, a que estos abusos puedan volver a ocurrir”, expresa Bustos Bottai.


Contar con reglas claras también es relevante para las propias instituciones encargadas de hacer cumplir la ley: permite entregar certeza sobre sus facultades y, al mismo tiempo, establecer mecanismos para prevenir abusos y determinar responsabilidades cuando la fuerza se utiliza fuera de los límites establecidos.


“Una regulación adecuada no debe entenderse como un obstáculo para la labor policial o militar. Por el contrario, reglas claras, compatibles con los derechos humanos y acompañadas de mecanismos efectivos de supervisión y rendición de cuentas permiten entregar mayor certeza a quienes ejercen funciones de seguridad y fortalecer la protección de todas las personas”, afirma Rodrigo Bustos Bottai.


Aspectos como la ausencia del principio de proporcionalidad, la falta de una prohibición expresa de apuntar armas menos letales al rostro, cabeza o torso y la eliminación del principio de rendición de cuentas; sumado a las disposiciones que amplían las circunstancias en que podría utilizarse fuerza potencialmente letal, incluida aquella destinada a impedir …

author: anred
title: Histórico: Buenos Aires será la sede del 40° Encuentro Plurinacional en 2027
content:
Tras cuatro décadas de recorrido federal y de manera ininterrumpida, el máximo evento de los feminismos y las disidencias regresa al territorio donde nació en 1986. La elección se realizó mediante el tradicional «aplausómetro» durante el cierre de la edición número 39 en Córdoba.

Por ANRed

 


CÓRDOBA — En una jornada cargada de mística, debate y organización colectiva, la Comisión Organizadora del 39° Encuentro Plurinacional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Bisexuales, Intersexuales y No Binaries anunció que la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires albergará la próxima edición del evento en 2027. La decisión se tomó a través del histórico sistema de «aplausómetro», el mecanismo asambleario y masivo con el que este espacio federal define democráticamente sus destinos año tras año. Tras la elección de la sede, se procedió a la lectura de las conclusiones de los más de 100 talleres que funcionaron durante el fin de semana.


Este regreso a las callee porteñas tiene una profunda carga simbólica y política. La última vez que el Encuentro se realizó en Buenos Aires fue en su edición fundacional de 1986. En aquel momento, apenas unas 600 mujeres provenientes de diferentes provincias y de diversas comunidades de pueblos originarios se congregaron para sembrar la semilla de una experiencia asamblearia y colectiva que terminaría transformando por completo la historia de los feminismos en la Argentina.


Cuarenta años después de aquella primera convocatoria, el espacio se ha masificado, transformado y complejizado. Con la única y lógica excepción del parate obligado por la pandemia de COVID-19, los Encuentros se sostuvieron de forma ininterrumpida durante cuatro décadas. Su persistencia en el tiempo consolida un formato único en el mundo: un espacio completamente autónomo de los gobiernos y los partidos, federal, plural, autofinanciado y autoconvocado que sirve como usina de organización, debate y posterior lucha en las calles.


De cara al próximo año, el desafío se traslada al centro político del país. En un contexto que demanda la articulación constante frente a las violencias y opresiones, el 40° Encuentro Plurinacional abrirá un nuevo capítulo en Buenos Aires con el objetivo de seguir reconociendo diversidades, compartiendo experiencias desde los territorios y fortaleciendo el tejido social hacia una comunidad más justa e igualitaria.


Todo en pleno año electoral, en el marco de una profunda crisis política social y cultural, en el gobierno de la Libertad Avanza. «Vamos a Buenos Aires a sacar a Milei, contra todos los fascismos. Seremos Nostres quienes les pongamos un freno a estas politicas de precarización de nuestras vidas» cerro una encuentrera.

author: Dyepeson Martins
title: Do susto ao mutirão: como a campanha de Lula tenta virar o jogo nas redes e nas ruas
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando

aqui

.


Falando por meio de um megafone, o presidente Lula (PT) anunciou, na quinta-feira (8), o primeiro ato público protagonizado por ele no segundo turno das eleições: uma passeata na manhã do dia seguinte, em Ceilândia, no Distrito Federal. O anúncio, publicado nas redes sociais, é encerrado com o brado de “bora, Lula!”, expressão vocal entre militantes e até então pouco ouvida na voz do petista. Embora com apenas 30 segundos,

o vídeo marcou o início de uma nova estratégia montada ao longo de uma semana repleta de embates na campanha à reeleição. Um comitê de crise precisou ser montado após o resultado inesperado no primeiro turno do pleito, em que a oposição elegeu a maioria no Senado Federal e o candidato da extrema-direita, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), saiu na frente, com uma diferença de 1,87 ponto percentual, equivalente a 2,2 milhões de votos válidos a mais do que o petista. 


Um dia depois da contabilização dos votos, a campanha petista já discutia a narrativa a ser adotada na comunicação e nas ruas até 25 de outubro

, quando os brasileiros voltarão às urnas. Mesmo com a discordância (ainda muito presente) entre a ala tradicional do PT e integrantes mais novos da base governista,

houve consenso sobre um aspecto considerado um erro durante o processo eleitoral: não dar a devida importância a formatos “virais” nas redes sociais por conta da enrijecida receita de campanha que preconiza um primeiro turno aprofundado em propostas e o segundo, direcionado ao desgaste do adversário. 


Para aliados ouvidos sob reserva pela

Agência Pública

, Lula teria admitido que a campanha não estava bem organizada. O presidente-candidato chegou a dizer ao presidente nacional do PT, Edinho Silva, que a observava como a

corrida eleitoral menos organizada em que participou desde 1989, quando disputou pela primeira vez a presidência da República. 


Para resolver os entraves e promover mudanças na linha de frente da campanha, o governador reeleito na Bahia, Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT), assumiu a coordenação de política (com ênfase na atração de prefeitos) e houve reforço na equipe de comunicação estratégica. O governador Rafael Fonteles (PT), reeleito no Piauí, foi escolhido para coordenar a comunicação. Além deles, o senador eleito, Rui Costa (PT-BA), assumiu a agenda; e o senador Camilo Santana (PT-CE) é o novo coordenador político, cargo anteriormente ocupado por Edinho Silva.


Também foram convocados para Brasília, em caráter de urgência, nomes progressistas engajados no Instagram, no YouTube, no TikTok e no WhatsApp. Entre eles, a deputada eleita Ana Elisa (PT), a segunda mais votada em Minas Gerais, que atribui 90% dos seus votos à presença ativa nas plataformas digitais. Além dela, outros jovens deputados federais eleitos engrossaram a campanha digital já em curso no segundo turno, como Jones Manoel (PSOL-PE), Guilherme Cortez (PSOL-SP), Renato Freitas (PT-PR) e Luna Zaratini (PT-SP).


De artistas fazendo o “L” ao “Exército de Lula” com Janones


O mutirão nas plataformas já sofreu ataques. Neste domingo (11), o ministro Kássio Nunes Marques atendeu ao pedido de Flávio Bolsonaro e mandou o WhatsApp suspender o canal “Exército de Lula”, administrado pelo deputado André Janones (Rede-MG) e que contabilizava mais de 3,4 milhões de seguidores. Marques justificou a suspensão por haver, segundo ele, a transmissão de conteúdo a milhões de pessoas “sob comando único para replicar conteúdos que a Corte já reconheceu como inverídicos”. Cerca de 4 horas depois, o corregedor do TSE, Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva, revogou a decisão e determinou o retorno provisório do canal. Cueva declarou, com preocupação, ter visto a interferência do presidente do TSE em um processo do qual não participa. De acordo com o corregedor, não foram apresentadas provas que justificassem a suspensão. A palavra final agora será do plenário do Tribunal.


Também nas redes sociais, de Anitta, Ivete Sangalo e Luan Santana, de Pabllo Vittar a Ludmilla, passando por cineastas, escritores e sambistas, mais de 200 nomes, desde o primeiro turno, têm feito vídeos e declarado apoio a Lula, um movimento que foi intensificado e cresceu nesta última semana. Somados, os nomes levantados pela reportagem totalizam mais de 400 milhões de seguidores nas redes sociais.

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: Administrador
title: Europa Zapatista. Dos Pronunciamientos: “La Casa y la Escuela”
content:
Dos Pronunciamientos: “La Casa y la Escuela” La Casa

No fue la foto de una mujer de 87 años, expulsada de su hogar de toda la vida, a la que sacaron de su casa en una camilla camino del hospital, la que rompió el muro por el que se desbordó la indignación. Fueron las imágenes que estaban dentro de esa imagen: familias expulsadas de sus casas porque los alquileres han subido tanto que no pueden pagarlos; hombres, mujeres, niños, expulsados de sus barrios, porque las élites financieras e inmobiliarias han decidido que las ciudades no son para vivir, sino el escenario teatral por el que circulen los turistas y compren, sobre todo compren, cualquier cosa, desde baratijas a modo de recuerdo, hasta cantidades ingentes de alcohol, paseando sus penurias por calles antes llenas de vida, de la vida de la gente que las habitaba.

No fue el nombre y la voz de Maricarmen, diciendo a las personas que, unas pocas horas antes de ser expulsada del lugar que llevaba habitando 70 años, estaban en la calle intentando impedir su desahucio, que siguieran luchando, no por ella, sino por todos, por todas, por una vivienda digna, por una ciudad habitable y por obligar a que se garantice el derecho de todos los ciudadanos a disfrutar de una vivienda digna y adecuada, mensaje que repitió después, ya desde el hospital. Fueron los nombres y las voces que están dentro del nombre de Maricarmen: Manuela, Andrés, Rosa, Ibrahim, Candela, Antonio, Rawda, Miguel, Emily, Nicolás y así hasta nombrar a los miles que perdieron sus casas sin tener ni un lugar digno dónde refugiarse; algunos, incluso perdieron la vida junto a la casa, porque no se veían viviendo y durmiendo a la intemperie.

No fueron solo los expulsados de sus casas, que es como decir de sus vidas; fue también la imposibilidad de tantos, de tantas, de conseguir una vivienda digna y asequible, de tener la posibilidad de vivir, de tan solo vivir. Fue la intranquilidad diaria de quienes hoy por hoy tienen un techo, pero no saben si lo tendrán mañana, porque igual conservarlo va a significar quedarse sin recursos para vivir la vida.

Las plazas se han llenado de tiendas de campaña, como imagen de un futuro que, de una forma u otra, nos alcanzará, como la imagen del único lugar en que podremos refugiarnos: la calle sin techo; solo que esta vez, esa última oportunidad de refugio se ha plantado en mitad de su escenario teatral, y ahora lo ve todo el mundo. Las acampadas en las plazas de un buen puñado de ciudades españolas, son al tiempo una denuncia y una recuperación del espacio para lo que siempre tuvo que ser, un lugar de encuentro entre personas, iguales y diferentes, que se ven, que se escuchan y se comparten.

En 1976, recién muerto el dictador Franco, el por entonces vicepresidente y ministro de Gobernación, Manuel Fraga, que años antes fue ministro en la dictadura, quiso evitar la celebración en las calles del primer Primero de Mayo en libertad, diciendo en voz alta lo que los “mandones” del poder económico y político pensaban antes y piensan ahora: “la calle es mía”. Pero no, la calle nunca fue suya, la calle es de todos, de todas, de todoas; la calle es el encuentro, la libertad, la lucha… Y las acampadas en las plazas son por todo eso, resumido en una vivienda justa, en la Vida y en la Dignidad.

Nota: Maricarmen murió en el hospital, catorce días después de ser desahuciada.

author: Nahuel Lag
title: Masabia: alimentos agroecológicos de una comuna santafesina con reconocimiento internacional
content:
Por Patricio Suárez Area


Ubicada sobre la ruta 33, a mitad de camino entre Rosario y Pujato, la localidad de Zavalla puede autodenominarse con orgullo una comuna en transición agroecológica desde hace 15 años, a partir de la

ordenanza que limitó las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos

 y la posterior creación de un tributo anual que respaldó a los productores para iniciar

el cambio de modelo productivo

. Los tiempos políticos cambiaron y el tributo se descontinuó, pero el cambio ya había iniciado. Sobre ese mapa periurbano sin fumigaciones,

un grupo de productores creó la Cooperativa de Trabajo Zavalla para levantar un viejo molino familiar

 e iniciar un camino que, en la actualidad, es de

producción de maíz, girasol y trigo agroecológico

. La estrella son los productos elaborados a partir del trigo bajo la

marca Masabia

 (harinas integrales, fideos frescos, fideos secos y pre pizzas sin agroquímicos), que fue reconocida por la FAO entre las nueve experiencias agroecológicas más destacadas del mundo.  


Una política pública que impulsó la agroecología


En 2011, la Comuna de Zavalla

promulgó la ordenanza (45/11)

 que prohíbe la radicación de depósitos de plaguicidas en el área urbana y suburbana, además de proscribir la circulación de vehículos cargados de agroquímicos. La norma crea

una zona de exclusión de aplicación aérea de 3.000 metros y de 800 metros terrestres en relación a la zona urbana

. Ese antecedente mereció el reconocimiento de la Red Nacional de Municipios y Comunidades que fomentan la Agroecología (Renama), que se acercó a la localidad y comenzó a colaborar con una decena de productores. En 2019, el Municipio de Zavalla se integró definitivamente a la Red.


A mediados de 2021, el gobierno comunal fue más allá y

 creó la tasa ambiental (en ese momento, de 600 pesos anuales) para financiar la transición agroecológica

. Los

fondos generados por la tasa ambiental permitían subsidiar a los productores

 —entonces, con 2.400.000 pesos al año, equivalente al costo de un arrendamiento—

para la compra de insumos, el pago del alquiler del campo donde se producía o para maquinaria específica para la producción agroecológica

.


La gestión del nuevo presidente comunal —Matías Suarez, del oficialismo santafesino; quien impidió la reelección de Guillermo Rajmil— derogó esa tasa. Sin embargo, y a pesar de todas las dificultades que van desde el plano local al nacional, los frutos de aquella política pública siguen vigentes.


Foto: Cooperativa agroecológica Zavalla


El ejido urbano de Zavalla ocupa alrededor de un cinco por ciento del territorio de la jurisdicción, el 95 por ciento restantes son tierras rurales aptas para la actividad agropecuaria primaria. De ellas,

200 hectáreas quedaron habilitadas para el desarollo agroecológico dentro de la zona de exclusión

. Nacida en 2021, al calor de la tasa ambiental, la Cooperativa de Trabajo Zavalla fue gestada por el productor Julián Graziosi, quien convocó a un grupo de pares para aprovechar el impulso comunal, el respaldo de la Renama y la contribución de la Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias de la Universidad Nacional de Rosario (FCA-UNR), sumada a la vinculación con el grupo ecologista Génesis.


“Había una política pública integral en respuesta al conflicto periurbano, basada en la construcción de una gobernanza responsable para producir alimentos a la vez que proteger el ambiente. Sobre todo, la salud de los residentes cuyas viviendas colindaban con lotes productivos”, explica Griselda Muñoz, directora de Género y Derechos Humanos de la FCA-UNR y presidenta de la Sociedad Argentina de Agroecología (SAAE).


Recuperar, producir, asociarse


En aquel 2021, Graziosi vio la oportunidad de poner en marcha un viejo molino familiar, que había quedado en desuso. El objetivo:

producir alimentos sanos, agregar valor en origen y generar fuentes laborales

 en la localidad. El paso siguiente fue alquilar 60 hectáreas dentro de las 200 que quedaron en la zona de exclusión. “Fueron años de mucho trabajo. Primero hubo que reacondicionar el molino y después empezar a producir, aprender, vender y seguir creciendo.

Hoy tenemos nuestra marca, hacemos harina integral y fuimos incorporando otros productos y comprando maquinarias para seguir agregando valor

”, cuenta Graziosi, presidente de la cooperativa.


Desde que pusieron el molino en marcha, en 2023, la cooperativa se fue posicionando en el mercado de productos orgánicos y agroecológicos y llegó a las góndolas …

title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?
