title: COP31 öncesi Pasifik’ten Antalya’ya çağrı: Taku Pakasoa Deklarasyonu
content:
Birleşmiş Milletler’in Kasım’da Antalya’da gerçekleşecek 31. Taraflar Konferansı (COP31) öncesi COP toplantıları Fiji’de tamamlandı. Toplantılar, Pasifik ülkelerinin öncülüğünde 5-8 Ekim tarihleri arasında gerçekleştirildi. 


Liderler, bakanlar ve üst düzey yetkililer, 6 Ekim’de Fiji’den iklim krizinin etkilerinden en yoğun şekilde etkilenen ülkelerden biri olan Tuvalu’ya seyahat gerçekleştirdi. Deniz seviyesinin yükselmesiyle Tuvalu, iklim krizinin etkilerinden dolayı dünyanın ilk "iklim mültecilerini" gönderen ülke olarak t

arihe geçmişti. 


Fiji Başbakanı Sitiveni Rabuka, Avustralya Başbakanı Anthony Albanese ile Nepal, Tuvalu, Palau ve Mauritius dahil iklim krizi karşısında savunmasız olan birçok ülkenin liderleri ve bakanları dikkat çeken açıklamalarda bulundu.


Fiji’deki toplantılardan ayrıca “Taku Pakasoa liderler deklarasyonu” çıktı. Deklarasyona adını veren “Taku Pakasoa”, Tuvalu'da birlik olmanın ve kolektif eylemde bulunmanın gücünü ifade ediyor. 


Deklarasyon, iklim krizinin Pasifik halkları, kültürleri ve geçim kaynakları üzerindeki ağır tehdidine karşı küresel bir eylem çağrısı olarak kayıtlara geçti. 


Deklarasyon, 1,5°C sıcaklık hedefinin korunması, devlet egemenliğinin ve deniz yetki alanlarının korunması ve iklim finansmanına erişimin artırılması gerekliliğine

vurgu yapıyor.


Deklarasyonda COP28 Küresel Envanter Değerlendirmesi'nin çağrısına atıf yapıldı. Bu doğrultuda; ülkelerin kendi koşullarına göre belirleyecekleri biçimde şu küresel çabalara katkıda bulunma taahhüdü yeniden teyit edildi: 


2030’a kadar yenilenebilir enerji kapasitesini üç katına çıkarmak,


2030’a kadar enerji verimliliği iyileştirmelerinin ortalama yıllık oranını iki katına çıkarmak,


Enerji sistemlerinde fosil yakıtlardan adil, düzenli ve hakkaniyetli bir şekilde uzaklaşmak, 


Bu kritik on yılda eylemi hızlandırarak 2050’ye kadar net sıfır’a ulaşmak, 


Ayrıca okyanusun iklim düzenleyici rolünün korunması ve okyanus ısınması ile deniz seviyesi yükselmesi gibi krizlere karşı kolektif eylem talepleri de yeniden dile getirildi.


COP31 öncesinde tüm taraflar iklim krizine karşı birleşmeye davet edildi.


BM Genel Sekreteri’nin Okyanus Özel Temsilcisi Peter Thomson, okyanusların müzakerelerin arka sıralarına atılmaması gerektiğin belirterek şunları aktardı:


“Türkiye bize, gezegenin ikliminin düzenlenmesinde okyanus-iklim ilişkisinin merkezi rolünü tanıyan bir Antalya Okyanus Deklarasyonu’nun hazırlanması için çalışacağını ve bundan sonra okyanus temelli iklim eylemlerini destekleyeceğini taahhüt etmiştir.” 


Fiji, Arazi ve Maden Kaynakları Bakanı Filimoni Vosarogo ise “Bugün iklim mimarisini sıfırdan tasarlıyor olsaydınız, gezegenin en büyük fazla ısı yutağını dışarıda bırakır mıydınız? Peki ya gezegenin en büyük aktif karbon rezervuarını?” diye sordu:


“Muhtemelen hayır. Oysa yaptığımız şey buna çok yakın. Okyanus, insanlık olarak saldığımız karbondioksitin yaklaşık dörtte birini ve hapsettiğimiz fazla ısının yüzde 90’ından fazlasını emmiştir. Okyanus, gezegenin iklim düzenleyicisi ve en büyük aktif karbon yutağı; dünyanın şu anda olduğundan çok daha sıcak olmamasının tek nedeni. Ve bu hizmetin bedelini kendi sağlığıyla ödüyor.”


Genel kurulda COP31 Müzakere Başkanı ve İklim Değişikliği ve Enerji Bakanı Chris Bowen, Tuvalu ve Fiji’deki gençlerin güçlü seslerini duyduklarını belirterek deklarasyonun COP31 için çok sağlam bir çıkış noktası sunduğunu söyledi.  


"Burada söylenenler COP31'e yön verecek"


Fiji Başbakanı Sitiveni Rabuka, liderlere “Her birimiz çözümün parçası olmak zorundayız” diye seslenerek birlik mesajı verdi:


“Taku Pakasoa’nın amacı da budur. Bölgelerimizi birleştirelim, çabalarımızı birleştirelim ortak zemin

bulalım.” 


Rabuka, “Burada, Pasifik’te ve dünyanın en büyük okyanusunun sesi gibi, amacımız inovasyon adaları yaratmak, çözümleri sergilemek ve yaygınlaştırmak ve sadece sorunun ölçüldüğü bir bölge olmaktan çıkıp çözümlerin paylaşıldığı bir yer haline gelmektir” dedi. 


Fiji lideri “Liderlerin bu salonda bu akşam söyledikleri, katılım sürecini şekillendirecek ve COP31 müzakerecilerine verilecek talimatlara yön verecek” uyarısında bulundu. 


Ayrıca Rabuka, Paris Anlaşması'nda belirlenen 1,5°C kritik eşiğinin aşımını sınırlandırma konusunda net bir uyarı yaptı:


“Hukuki yükümlülüklerimize ve ahlaki hedeflerimize aykırı olan aşımı sınırlamaya kararlı olduğumuzu açık ve net biçimde göstermeliyiz.”

title: Rechenzentren (im KI-Boom) und die katastrophalen Umweltauswirkungen der Digitalisierung
content:
Dossier


„…

Die ETC Group leistet mit „Hinter den Wolken – Die Umweltauswirkungen der Digitalisierung“ einem neuen Bericht über die schwerwiegenden ökologischen und sozialen Risiken der Digitaltechnik, einen Beitrag zu dieser Debatte. Wir haben festgestellt, dass die Digitalisierung bestehende Ungleichheiten verschärft und eine immer stärkere Ausbeutung von Ressourcen aus der Erde, den Ozeanen und dem Weltraum erfordert. (…) Daten sind weder ätherisch noch harmlos. Sie sind ressourcenintensiv, bestehen aus Sand, Wasser, Kohle und schädlichen Chemikalien, die giftige Abfälle erzeugen. Für die Herstellung von Halbleiterchips, dem Baustein aller digitalen Dinge, werden beispielsweise Quarzsand, Quarz und hochreines Wasser benötigt. Die Fabriken für diese Chips werden auf großen Flächen gebaut, und es ist nachgewiesen, dass die Arbeiter dort schädlichen Chemikalien ausgesetzt sind

…“ span.

Meldung vom 4.9.2024 der ETC Group


 zum Bericht „Detrás de las nubes“ und mehr dazu, auch am Beispiel Lateinamerika:


Kampf um Wasser: Rechenzentren boomen – Bundesregierung will Umweltvorgaben lockern


„In Deutschland entstehen immer mehr Rechenzentren. CORRECTIV zeigt: Viele stehen ausgerechnet dort, wo Wasser im Sommer knapp wird. Ihre Abwärme verpufft meist ungenutzt. Trotzdem will die Bundesregierung die Umweltvorgaben für die Branche lockern. (…) Eine entsprechende Novelle des Energieeffizienzgesetzes wird derzeit im Bundestag beraten. Zum Beispiel soll das Zieldatum für die hundertprozentige Versorgung von Rechenzentren mit erneuerbaren Energien nach hinten verschoben werden. Außerdem sollen Betreiber Abwärme künftig nicht mehr zwingend nutzen müssen. Dabei zeigt eine CORRECTIV-Auswertung des neuen Rechenzentrenregisters des Bundeswirtschaftsministerium

, dass schon die bestehenden Anlagen Ressourcenfragen aufwerfen…“

Beitrag von Katarina Huth, Elena Kolb und Philipp Waack vom 08. Oktober 2026 bei Correctiv


 – siehe hingegen aus Österreich:


Fünf Forderungen für eine sozial-ökologische Rechenzentrumspolitik


„Rechenzentren werden mittlerweile als kritische Infrastruktur verhandelt. Doch warum, wo und wie diese gebaut werden, auf welche Energie- und Wasserressourcen sie zurückgreifen und wem sie schlussendlich nützen, ist Aushandlungssache. Dieser Beitrag stellt fünf Forderungen für eine sozial-ökologische Rechenzentrumspolitik vor, die solche Fragen demokratisch beantwortet. Ausgangspunkt ist ein kürzlich im Kurswechsel vorgestelltes Forschungs- und Handlungsprogramm für eine sozial-ökologisch planende Wirtschaftspolitik, das an Eduard März’ Arbeiten – im Anschluss an John Maynard Keynes und Karl Marx – anschließt und die Idee eines demokratischen, dritten Wegs zwischen Markt- und Planwirtschaft aufgreift. (…) 1. Rechenzentrumssektor klimaverträglich umbauen: (…) Bei Rechenzentren stammen die meisten Treibhausgasemissionen aus dem Energieverbrauch für Strom und Kühlung. Rechenzentren müssen daher als eigenständiger Sektor begriffen werden, der klimaverträglich umgebaut werden muss. Damit Rechenzentren erneuerbaren Strom beziehen können, braucht der Energiesektor einen beschleunigten Ausbau erneuerbarer Energien, der Stromnetze sowie der Speicher- und Flexibilitätsoptionen. In dem Zuge müssen die Fernwärmenetze modernisiert werden, damit sich auch die niedrigtemperierte Abwärme von Rechenzentren einspeisen lassen kann. (…) 2. Betreiber in die Pflicht nehmen: Makroökonomische Stellschrauben zielen darauf ab, den Ausbau von Rechenzentren durch gezielte staatliche Regulierung und Steuerung in gesellschaftlich orientierte Bahnen zu lenken. Dafür sollte Steuerpolitik sicherstellen, dass große Rechenzentrumsbetreiber einen angemessenen finanziellen Beitrag an ihren Standorten, insbesondere kleineren Gemeinden, leisten, in denen sie erhebliche Flächen-, Energie- und Infrastrukturressourcen beanspruchen. (…) Entgegen der Kultur der permanenten Verfügbarkeit könnten Rechenzentren dazu verpflichtet werden, ihre Stromnachfrage möglichst flexibel an Zeiten hoher Wind- und Solarstromproduktion anzupassen, denn insbesondere nicht zeitkritische Anwendungen (z. B. Backups, wissenschaftliche Forschung, KI-Training) können zeitlich verschoben werden. (…) 3. Bedarf und Kontrolle demokratisch aushandeln: (…) Rechenkapazitäten sollten an einen demokratisch verhandelten Bedarf geknüpft werden – an die Frage, welche KI und Software wir überhaupt betreiben wollen. So ist für ein spezialisiertes KI-Modell, z. B. zur Hautkrebs-Erkennung …

author: winter oak
title: Our righteous struggle
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


You’ve got to fight for what you want

For all that you believe

It’s right to fight for what we want

To live the way we please

As long as we have done our best

Then no-one can do more

And life and love and happiness

Are well worth fighting for


These lyrics, together with the stirring tune to which they are set, made a great impression on me when I was a boy.


The song

Fight

 by The Musketeers, released as a single in 1969, was the

theme music

 for

The Flashing Blade

, the English version of a French TV series called

Le Chevalier Tempête

. [1]


The story is based on historical events during the 17th century War of the Mantuan Succession between France and Spain, but I do not think the details of the plot interested me much – it was the song that I loved!


I knew somehow – in my bones, in my blood, in my guts – that what the words were saying was both true and important.


The song’s message was still ringing in my ears when I first launched myself, as a teenager, into my ongoing – but so far unsuccessful – efforts to bring down the venal and usurious globalist system.


I must have already come across the same spirit in the tales of Robin Hood, William Tell and other heroes and so I suppose one could argue that the outlook had been implanted in me by the cultural environment in which I grew up.


But I would say, rather, that it was already there at my birth – in the innate pattern of my mind, heart and soul – and that external stimuli like the song merely activated a thought that was waiting to be thought, provided the means by which an unconscious attitude became conscious.


And, even though not everyone thinks that way, I would say that we are looking here at an idea – a principle, rather – that generally forms part of our collective culture, in Europe and elsewhere.


We see it, for instance, in medieval Norse culture, in the

Elder Edda

 of Saemund Sigfusson:


“A cowardly man thinks he will ever live, if warfare he avoids; but old age will give him no peace, though spears may spare him”.

 [2]


It is also present, of course, in the Arthurian legends, as I noticed when re-reading a book that I have kept hold of since my childhood –

King Arthur and His Knights of the Round Table

 by Roger Lancelyn Green (1918-1987), a friend and

biographer

 of the author C.S. Lewis. [3]


Although this was published by Penguin under the “Puffin” label aimed at younger readers, it is a serious and eloquent re-telling based on Sir Thomas Malory’s famous account and weaving in material from various other sources.


I was amused to see the title of the aforementioned TV series make an appearance when Merlin the magician/druid announces, regarding young Arthur: “In Avalon the elves are forging Excalibur to be the sword of his right – the clean flashing blade that shall be raised only in the cause of right, shining on the earth until the time comes when they shall call it back again”. [4]


Likewise, Sir Launcelot of the Lake tells Sir Percivale of Wales: “Not in great deeds of arms lies the true worth of knighthood – rather in the heart of the doer of such deeds: if he be pure and humble, doing all things to the glory of God and to bring that glory and that peace throughout our holy kingdom of Logres”. [5]


At the inauguration of the Round Table, Merlin declares: “All of you, and those who shall sit afterwards at this Table, are the Knights of Logres, and for the glory of Logres, the Realm of Righteousness, do not ever depart from the high virtues of this realm.


“Do no outrage nor murder nor any cruel or wicked thing; fly from treason and all untruthfulness and dishonest dealing; give mercy unto those who seek it – or sit no more at this Table.


“And always give all the help in your power to ladies and damsels, go out to succour gentlewomen and widows, turn from all else to right any wrong done to any woman in the world – and never, on pain of death and eternal disgrace, do you any ill thing to a woman, or suffer it to be done. Nor, for love or gain, fight in any quarrel that is not just and righteous”. [6]


By the way, the sign of Logres – “the land of true good and piety, nobleness and right living” [7] – is described by Lancelyn Green as being a five-pointed star [8] like the one that forms the organic radical logo below, together, in our case, with the rising sun of renewal and the greenery of life.

title: Extreme Weather Disasters Cost Hundreds of Billions. Let’s Make Polluters Pay.
content:
As the Trump administration guts disaster aid, it’s time for an extreme weather superfund paid for by fossil fuel firms.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

One of the most visible consequences of global warming is the increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, such as the powerful nor’easter that hammered the East Coast and mid-Atlantic for several days in late September with heavy rain, winds, and flooding. Indeed, a wide array of scientific studies over the past couple of decades have shown how human-caused climate change affects the intensity, frequency, and impact of extreme weather — from wildfires in the U.S. and Australia to record-setting flooding in China. And now, a major study prepared by two dozen scientists from across the globe has found a link between industrial emissions and the warming of the snow-capped Himalayan region that led to the collapse of the glacier that caused the catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet last month, in which over 1,300 people were killed while thousands are still missing.

In light of such developments, programs designed to address climate disasters are urgently needed. In the interview that follows, economist Michael Ash makes the case for the establishment of an Extreme Weather Superfund to protect U.S. communities from extreme weather events like those discussed above. Ash is professor of economics and public policy and co-director of the Corporate Toxics Information Project at the Political Economy Research Institute (PERI) at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

C.J. Polychroniou: This past summer was the hottest on record in the United States as well as in western Europe. Indeed, new data shows that global warming is accelerating and the UN says that exceeding the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal above pre-industrial levels looks now unavoidable. As such, extreme weather events like last month’s nor’easter storm that produced strong winds, large waves, and coastal flooding along the East Coast, and Hurricane Helene, which ripped across the U.S. Southeast two years ago and was responsible for at least 250 fatalities, are expected to become more intense. Yet, instead of increasing funding for extreme weather, the Trump administration has actually slashed disaster aid programs and gutted agencies whose mission is to protect communities against extreme weather disasters. Can you talk a bit about the problem at hand with extreme weather events?

Michael Ash: Top weather and climate disasters, typically hurricanes, have costs running into hundreds of billions of dollars. In addition to its war on climate policy, the Trump administration has been utterly derelict in protecting communities from extreme weather disasters or rebuilding after disasters.

Hurricane Helene brought horrendous damage to uplands North Carolina, making very clear that the impact of climate change will not be limited to low-lying coastal areas. Immediately after becoming president in 2025, Donald Trump went around North Carolina saying, “the days of betrayal and neglect are over,” while simultaneously planning to institutionalize betrayal and neglect by getting rid of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), remarking: “If it was up to me right now, I’d end it right now.”

The Trump administration squeezed out 4,300 staff from FEMA in 2025. Its plan to reduce another 11,000 employees this year has been stopped by the courts for now. FEMA’s capacity is degraded. As The Nation article recounts, the North Carolina recovery funds have been delivered in an ineffective trickle.

How should we explain the Trump administration’s complete disregard of the risks associated with extreme weather events, which should be of deep concern to voters in the upcoming midterm elections?

It fits important patterns: climate denialism in service to fossil fuel companies; callous disregard for human suffering; and federal abdication of responsibility for the general welfare.

How much more likely and how much more destructive are episodes of extreme heat or rainfall, droughts, or hurricanes because of climate change? The science is increasingly precise and clear. Attribution science — the subject of a terrific new National Academies publication, “The Attribution of Extreme Weather and Climate Events and Their Impacts” (2026) — can establish with …

author: Chinedu Akpa
title: Marketing GLP-1 Drugs for Addiction: Why Critics Are Skeptical
content:
T

he enthusiasm surrounding glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) has moved beyond diabetes and obesity. Scientists are now investigating whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide could help treat addiction by reducing cravings and altering the brain circuits involved in reward.


There is a

biological rationale

 for this idea. GLP-1 receptors are present in brain regions involved in reward, motivation, learning, and behavior. Early research suggests that GLP-1RAs may influence some of the same pathways implicated in addictive behavior.


But addiction is more than a biological process. It also has psychological and social dimensions. People may use substances or engage in compulsive behaviors to cope with trauma, loneliness, shame, anxiety, stress, or difficult environments. Recovery can therefore require more than suppressing a craving: it can involve developing new coping mechanisms, rebuilding relationships, changing one’s environment, and learning to live without the behavior that once served a psychological function.


That raises a question that has received less attention amid the excitement over GLP-1 drugs: if a medication reduces the biological urge to use a substance, does that necessarily mean it has treated the addiction? Or has it simply created an opportunity for the person to begin addressing the deeper psychological and social factors underlying the behavior?


There are also unresolved questions about the long-term effects of manipulating neural pathways involved not only in reward and craving, but also in motivation, pleasure, and affect. While current regulatory assessments and randomized trials have not established a causal link between GLP-1RAs and serious psychiatric harms, observational and pharmacovigilance studies have generated signals that warrant further investigation.


Image created with AI


A long-running debate


That tension is reflected in a long-running debate over the role of willpower and personal agency in addiction. If addiction is driven largely by changes in brain circuitry, then framing recovery in terms of choice, discipline, or self-control can seem simplistic. But clinicians who work with people in recovery argue that acknowledging addiction’s biological basis does not eliminate the need for personal agency or the psychological work of recovery.


“It is not a matter of willpower or discipline” has become the rallying cry of advocates of prescribing glucagon-like peptide receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) for addiction. The argument is that these drugs act on the neurobiology of hunger, satiety, cravings, and reward—processes that may operate beyond deliberate self-control.


But

Brook McKenzie

 does not quite agree with this notion. The licensed chemical dependency counselor who has spent over a decade with families and individuals struggling with substance use disorder is convinced that willpower and discipline have a role to play in recovery. The counselor believes the real question isn’t whether willpower or discipline matter, but what they can accomplish. While he notes that these human traits are essential, he adds that “it is not all that is required, but they could open the door to recovery.”


Dr. Lauren Grawert

, a double board-certified addiction psychiatrist, similarly argues that recovery requires repeated acts of commitment and accountability.


“It takes discipline and willpower to repeat many of the same challenging decisions: attending therapy sessions, adhering to the medication regimen as ordered by their doctor, avoiding risky behaviors, mending damaged relationships and practicing coping mechanisms to avoid giving into cravings. These types of decision-making require commitment and accountability. There is a need for a middle ground to exist in addiction treatment.”


The debate over willpower, however, is only one part of a larger disagreement about how addiction should be understood. If addiction is viewed primarily through a biological lens, it follows that changing the brain’s reward circuitry could be seen as a powerful way to treat it. But research on addiction has long suggested that biology is only part of the story.


The biological rationale: Why GLP-1s are being studied for addiction


It is not surprising that GLP-1RAs are being investigated for use in addiction. Over the years, this class of medication’s therapeutic use has expanded beyond its initial indication for diabetes to areas such as obesity, renal …

title: Inside the successful campaign against illegal Chinese mining in Africa
content:
This article

Inside the successful campaign against illegal Chinese mining in Africa

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


When the shrill of heavy earthmoving machinery crept towards Elias Mlambo’s riverside banana plantations in February, the sudden brownish color of the river alarmed him. 


The water was laced with used machinery oil, disfiguring the once crystal-clear, wild water of the

Haroni River

. The river not only sustains the Ndau tribal people of the Chimanimani district in southeast Zimbabwe but also acts as Zimbabwe’s eastern border with Mozambique. By December of last year, excavators operated by a

Chinese mining syndicate

 were at work along a stretch of the riverbeds — tearing

up centuries of riparian ecology in a hunt for alluvial gold deposits.


“They appeared without notice, without our permission, claiming to have a government license to dig for gold on our land, but never showing the actual permit,” said Mlambo, a banana farmer and local tribal elder in

Rusitu

, one of the largest villages in the district. 


He said he confronted a man who claimed to be the manager of the Chinese miners — but the man gave his name only as “Xai Samson” and flatly refused to give out the company’s name. He acted as though he did not understand English — a deliberate tactic some dubious Chinese mining syndicates adopt in Zimbabwe when confronted by aggrieved locals, Mlambo said. 


“He just waffled a few sentences in Chinese — gestured to the excavators and piles of fresh soil,” he explained. “We figured out that our river, fruit plantations and ancestral graves were collateral to the invaders.” 


Ignored at first


For the next three months, Mlambo made complaints to the

Chimanimani municipal

 authorities, a lawmaker and Zimbabwe’s mines ministry — and was ignored. Just one ministry bureaucrat responded to Mlambo and other tribal elders by telephone, only to say that his hands were tied, citing how high-level state partnerships and national economic priorities trump tribal land rights. It’s a familiar

cold response

 from Zimbabwe’s government that human rights leaders say has given dozens of Chinese prospectors carte blanche to excavate hills and river streams, and encroach onto tribal farming and grazing lands in pursuit of precious metals like platinum, lithium or gold.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


“There’s a cozy, transactional relationship between state decision-makers and Chinese minerals prospectors,” said

Nsama Musonda

, the executive director of Care for Nature Zambia, a regional ecology monitoring nonprofit. “This gifts Chinese businesspeople a carefree right to dig for precious minerals — without consent — on tribal people’s lands in Zimbabwe and nearby countries like Zambia.” 


Knowing the script that has played out elsewhere across Zimbabwe, Mlambo and fellow villagers refused to retreat. Instead, they looked across the international boundary to Mozambique — a stone’s throw across the Haroni River. On the other side, in Mozambique’s

Sussundenga district

, villager Manuel Pinto was watching his community’s primary fish stocks float belly-up to the surface.


Fish in the community ponds that line the Mozambique side of the Haroni riverbed were suffocating from the sludge coming from the spoiled headwaters on the Zimbabwe side, he said. But Pinto feared something worse: Mozambique’s community health nurses warned that children could develop

chemical rashes

 if they encountered contaminated waters. 


“The river doesn’t need a passport to flow and nourish both countries, Zimbabwe and Mozambique,” he said, speaking the same

Ndau vernacular language

 that hundreds of thousands of

tribal people on the Zimbabwe side of the river border speak, too. “We realized that if authorities in Zimbabwe would not enforce environmental law, the Ndau people on both sides of the border would act to protect their right to safe livelihoods.”


The border alliance 


Pinto says he knew routine complaints would be easily ignored by state decision-makers. So Mlambo and Pinto conjured up a community alliance rooted in their shared Ndau lineage. Tribal identity, older than colonial state borders, drove their determination to defend their environment against the encroachment of heavily polluting Chinese miners

. 


In daylight, the Ndau communities on the Zimbabwe side confronted the Chinese miners: spraying graffiti on the …

author: Unknown
title: Jeff Shantz - From Climate Crisis to Climate Culling
content:
Author

: Jeff Shantz

Title

: From Climate Crisis to Climate Culling

Subtitle

: Dis-Ecologies of Snuff Capital

Date

: 1996, Summer

Source

: Scanned from Anarcho-Syndicalist Review #94, Summer, 2026


 We have entered a period which I have taken to calling snuff capitalism—accumulation by elimination. Capital has moved past the mere accumulation by dispossession that David Harvey has written about extensively. Beyond dispossession, which Harvey argues clears routes for capital circulation, capital has moved to eliminate anything and everything that might pose a drain on accumulation (anything that might “waste” a penny for capital). This includes even minimal social spending that might support poor and unemployed working-class people, such as social housing, unemployment benefits, welfare, health care, etc. Increasingly it involves eliminating the poor and unemployed themselves—those deemed by capital to be useless to production or consumption —as through assisted suicide and elimination of supports for drug users (safe supply, harm reduction) or unhoused people such that the expected outcome is most likely death. It can include removal of health and safety protections for workers (in industries where capital believes those workers can be readily replaced). War, of course, remains a key means for capital to kill people.


 Capitalist eliminationism also includes active pursuit of ecocide. This is occurring through the elimination of regulations on industry, opening previously protected natural spaces for extraction, conversion of land into pesticide wastelands for industrial farming, mining of the seas and oceans, etc. We see numerous examples, such as the Trump regime’s plans to open pristine areas for oil drilling, as in the Arctic. Perversely, the United States government has formed a committee that has the power to decide when extinction is acceptable. The Endangered Species Committee—colloquially known as the God Squad—was created under the Endangered Species Act. It can exempt projects from law when protecting a species interferes with major economic interests. After three decades without meeting, the committee recently approved drilling in the Gulf of Mexico that could lead to extinction of the critically endangered Rice’s whale (only 51 of which are still alive).


 Ecocidal eliminationism also includes new wars and occupations. The recently launched Israel-US war on Iran is causing immense ecological crises in addition to the thousands of people murdered in the imperialist assault. I will address this in detail in an upcoming article.


 Climate crises provide opportunities for eliminationism on mass scales at accelerated pace. For capital, it is a low-cost way for clearing away human and natural obstacles to accumulation. And it allows them to do so in a way that permits them to make claims of blamelessness (as opposed to wars for example).


 Most of the people and places most severely impacted by climate crises are poor— excluded from production and consumption for capital by regimes of enforced scarcity. While reasonable people would view this as an atrocity, and reason to more quickly address climate destruction, for capital it is a boon—and reason to allow, or even encourage, climate crises to occur, and occur more precipitously.


 Entire regions and areas are designated for culling. Mike Davis refers to national sacrifice zones, “using this term to think about the ecological disaster to which certain regions of the US have been relegated, since neither these spaces nor their inhabitants are considered to be productive elements of the capitalist system.” (Sayak Valencia, 2018,

Gore Capitalism

. South Pasadena: Semiotext(e), p. 182)


Accelerating Past the Point...


 There are more and more indications that some of the world’s tipping points, such as drastic changes to ocean currents, could be breached in a future that is no longer very distant. Today’s rate of global warming—more than 1.3 degrees C (2.3 degrees F) in only the last hundred years—is already completely unprecedented in human history.


 And it is only getting worse. Global warming is accelerating, going from 1.4 to 1.6 degrees C in 2023 to two degrees C and rising by the 2030s. It could blow past two degrees before the end of the century. New research published in March 2026 in Geophysical Research Letters, finds that the rate of global warming has accelerated since 2015, even after accounting for other phenomena such as …

author: Austin Corona
title: The bipartisan energy bill tearing the climate movement apart
content:
In order to solve climate change, you have to do two things — stop burning fossil fuels, and build clean energy to replace them. The last few decades in the United States have witnessed a long back-and-forth over which of the two goals is more important, and over how to achieve either of them. Is it more important to pass a carbon tax, or subsidize electric vehicles? To block a new oil pipeline, or build a lot of solar and wind? 


On this question, the coalition known as the climate movement has fractured into two broad groups. On one side, there are activists, lawyers, and environmentalists, who tend to focus on blocking and reducing fossil fuel use. On the other, there are renewable energy companies and policy wonks, who tend to focus on building more clean energy.


These factions have clashed in the past, but over the past week a kind of civil war has erupted between the different elements of the climate movement. The inciting incident was the release of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a long-awaited Senate bill that is designed to enable the construction of more power plants, transmission lines, and gas pipelines. The bill does this by weakening some of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws, speeding up the timeline for government agencies to issue permits, and making it harder to cancel projects that have already gotten federal approval. 


For climate-conscious supporters of the bill, it’s better for the planet to build a lot of clean energy even if it means some fossil fuels get built as well, and even if they cause some damage to the environment on the way. Supporters of the effort argue that if the U.S. builds out new clean capacity, it will be easier to wean off fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming and all its myriad consequences. Opponents say that’s a Faustian bargain, one that will jeopardize tribal nations, other marginalized communities, and endangered species.


“It is definitely exposing a potential fault line between the environmental community and clean energy interests,” said Representative Jared Huffman, a Democrat who represents Northern California, in an interview with Grist. 


Representative Jared Huffman, a Democrat from California, is skeptical of the Senate permitting reform bill.


Photo by Andrew Harnik / Getty Images


BAAJA is the product of months of bipartisan negotiation between four members of the Senate committees focused on energy and the environment. The two Democrats in the talks were Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who are both climate hawks and clean energy advocates. The Republicans were Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who are advocates of fossil fuels and critics of environmental regulation. Despite their ideological differences, the four senators managed to reach a compromise on a

sprawling 400-page bill

 with hundreds of individual provisions. 


The so-called “four corners” reached a deal just before Congress left for its fall recess, and the Senate will not return to take up the bill until after the midterm elections. The bill has not even made it through committee yet, and it also faces an uncertain fate in the House of Representatives. The next few weeks will see a scramble of lobbying as supporters and opponents of the bill try to sway senators and representatives for or away from the bill.


So far, at least, the builders seem to have more influence than the blockers, at least within the climate movement. President Donald Trump has spent the last two years

repealing


most


federal


climate policy

 and blocking the development of new clean energy, and many climate advocates seem willing to accept an imperfect deal rather than hold out hope of fixing Trump’s damage after he leaves office.


“It’s a lot easier to prevent things from being built than to build things, and that applies both to fossil fuels and to renewables,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate expert at the science nonprofit Berkeley Earth, who also directs climate research for the tech company Stripe. “I don’t want us to run roughshod over any community, but we also can’t give everyone a veto for an issue as important as climate change. So ultimately, we need to strike a balance there.”


The case in favor: Build more


A big challenge with building clean energy is that it takes up a lot of space. Solar farms and wind farms can cover thousands of acres of land, and the …

author: Johnnie Jae
title: Indigenous People Are Resisting Erasure From Schools, Media, and Our Land
content:
Joining the fight against our erasure helps Native communities defend our right to be seen, heard, and counted.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas that the Indigenous Lucayan people called Guanahani. He continued on to Cuba and Hispaniola and, on later voyages, to other parts of the Caribbean, but he never set foot in what is now the continental United States. It makes little sense for a country to honor a man who never reached it, and even less to credit him with discovering a place that millions of people already called home. And it makes even less given what Columbus actually did in the places where he stepped foot: He rounded up Indigenous people in the Caribbean, chained them, and sent them as slaves to Spain. And when Indigenous communities rose up in resistance, he ordered his soldiers to “spread terror,” maiming and slaughtering civilians en masse using firearms, dogs, swords, and pikes.

But despite all this, in 1937, the United States established a federal holiday in his name anyway.

Native people have been fighting the sanitization of Columbus’s story for decades. The idea of replacing Columbus Day arose as early as 1977, when Indigenous representatives raised it at a United Nations conference in Geneva.

In 1990, South Dakota renamed the day Native Americans’ Day. The change began with Oglala Lakota newspaper publisher Tim Giago, whose columns challenged Governor George Mickelson to mark the centennial of the Wounded Knee massacre with a “Year of Reconciliation” and to give the October holiday to Native people, proposals Mickelson took to tribal leaders and then to the legislature.

Two years later, as the country marked 500 years since Columbus landed, the city of Berkeley, California, adopted Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Bay Area Native organizers and their allies, returning from a 1990 gathering of Indigenous nations in Quito, Ecuador, formed a coalition called Resistance 500 and won official taskforce status from the City Council, which then unanimously adopted their recommendation to replace Columbus Day. Today at least 17 states and more than 100 cities recognize it, and in 2021, Joe Biden became the first president to formally proclaim it.

Then, the next White House reversed course. In October 2025, President Trump moved to “reclaim” Columbus’s legacy from those he termed “left-wing arsonists,” though he never mentioned Indigenous Peoples’ Day by name.

Native people have been fighting the sanitization of Columbus’s story for decades.

Columbus Day tells a story that skips what came before 1492 and what came after. Before the United States existed, Indigenous nations governed and cared for these lands. Colonization brought land theft, forced removal, and government policies designed to break those nations and sever Native people from their languages, cultures, communities, and homelands.

The people carrying out those policies often stated their intentions openly. In 1851, California’s first governor, Peter Burnett, told state legislators that a war of extermination would continue “until the Indian race becomes extinct.” In 1892, Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, described the purpose of federal boarding schools in one line: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.”

Indigenous Peoples’ Day marks that failure. It also arrives during a new wave of attempted erasure across Indian Country. The methods are different, but the questions are familiar. Who gets counted? Who gets to tell our history? Who gets to speak for Native people? Who decides what happens to Indigenous land, water, and culture?

When this country attempts to count Native people, it always seems to fall short. Pollsters ostensibly skip us because oursample size is too small to report. On election night in 2020, a national network put Native voters on screen as “something else.”

The U.S. census, for all its flaws, at least asks. It lets us check a box and write in the name of our tribe.

Now the federal government wants to stop asking altogether. On September 10, 2026, the Census Bureau proposed dropping the race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 census. Race has been on the form since the first count in 1790, though for much of that time we were left out. Until 1940, the government excluded “Indians …

author: Poetry Collection
title: The Arrogance of Man by Julia Caitlin Miller
content:
Trigger warning: Brief mention of rape and suicide.


Thighs soaked in period blood


I spent eight hours, free bleeding


Part of it in restraints, after a


Flashback to being raped


But, I don’t know how to articulate it


It’s just from the way a group of men


Grabbed, squeezed and held down my wrists


They were just following protocol


But, why don’t they think of this…


That restraints can be traumatic?


Once released, I stay in my room


Until I march to the nurses station


And wave my bloody underwear in the air


What do I have to do to get a pad around here?


Stamp on the label difficult


So much trauma, I can’t communicate it


In a language that humans understand


But, the doctor blames it all on bipolar disorder


I’m far gone, but not in the way he thinks


It’s all performance art


Song requests to the radio stations with dedications


Notes on the paper trash bags for the janitors


Notes on the paper menu trays for everyone in the kitchen


The nurse is the only one who gets me


My own Nurse Jackie


Because she’s on the same wavelength


And doesn’t misunderstand me


She doesn’t have the arrogance


Or stigmatize me the same way as my doctor


I told him I felt addicted to Effexor


He just said “that’s not in the literature”


As if books have all the answers


Medical students in and out of the unit


Adding to the rumble and all of the noise


My mind is like a sponge that just absorbs


Every piece of information in the background


The downloads are too much at once


And my system crashes out


But, if I need time alone from this


I’m not social enough


The kid that tried to hang himself


Was practically out the next day


No snacks for the diabetic kid


The woman with the urostomy bag got an infection


Because they weren’t on top of it


My doctor screams at me


Pounds his fists on my bedroom door


Another patient had to intervene


But, we’re not allowed to change doctors here


I just curled up into a ball on the floor


And started sobbing


A fire breaks out in the kitchen


The unit fills with smoke


They wouldn’t open a window for us


I guess it’s fine to breathe in the smokey air


Because it’s just “protocol”


As if laws are always moral


They finally opened an office window for us


While patients waited in a state of panic


Years, after I’ve left


They’ll release Daniel Prude too soon


And not get enough blame


And not take enough accountability


There was only one protest against the hospital


They have blood on their hands


But god forbid, someone says it


They’ll be practically immune


And that’s the arrogance of man


Society only accepts certain elements of mental illness


But, I’ve had the “ugly” and “messy” parts of it


Doctors are not educated enough on


Medical Trauma or the troubled teen industry


And some will simply point their fingers at us


Instead of the mental health care system or cops


Or the lack of advancement


The treatment that is supposed to help


Can actually make the illness worse


And there needs to be a better term than


Non-compliance because it doesn’t explain


The nuances


There’s a fucking crisis in this country


And now Trump wants to bring back


Mental institustions


Where atrocities and deaths have occurred,


While, I’m still paying for therapy to


Undo the damage hospitals did


I’m about to unleash my inner menace


But, who is going to believe us,


The mental patients, anyway?


I wanted to start a petition when I got out of the hospital


But Zyprexa took the life out of me


Now, I stew on it


I stew on the memories


So this is my testimony


If I ever go crazy again,


Skip Strong Hospital and send me to


Rochester General instead


* * *


Born in secrecy and placed for adoption, Julia Caitlin Miller spent her childhood drawing on floors with toothpaste. She has been published in “The Mighty” and “The Relinquished Review.” She currently lives in artist housing with her two cats, Kitten & Smokey.


Return to Poetry Collection

The Arrogance of Man by Julia Caitlin Miller

 appeared first on

Mad In America

.

author: Unknown
title: Antiterro et psychiatrie : un bref récap de la loi Rodwell
content:
Quelques infos sur la loi Rodwell, ou loi Philippine, passée fin juillet 2026


La loi Rodwell ou loi Philippine (oui oui, Philippine comme la meuf assassinée par un type sortant de

CRA

 en septembre 2024, provoquant une campagne de haine raciste et xénophobe), ou loi du 27 juillet 2026, est une loi qui mixe le droit pénal, le droit de la santé et le droit des étrangers pour «

 

prévenir le passage à l'acte terroriste

 

» - ambiance minority report.


Pour résumer, c'est un renforcement ou une adaptation de mesures répressives qui étaient déjà souvent présentes - et mises en place - dans le droit français : il y a peu de choses complètement nouvelles. On trouve intéressant d'analyser ici quelques unes de ses principales mesures, notamment du fait des liens étroits entre répression et psychiatrie, qui sont très explicites dans la loi.


La loi met en place :


1) Une rétention de sûreté terroriste à l'issue de la peine : enfermement d'une personne dans des établissements «

 

socio-médico-judiciaires de sûreté

 

» après l'exécution complète de sa peine. Cette mesure concernerait les personnes condamnées à une peine d'au moins quinze ans pour un crime de terrorisme. Une commission, peu avant la fin de la peine, doit déterminer si la personne présente une «

 

particulière dangerosité

 

», concept carrément flou évalué notamment sur des critères encore plus flous comme le «

 

risque de récidive

 

», «

 

l'adhésion persistante à une idéologie terroriste

 

» et un «

 

trouble grave de la personnalité

 

»...


Comme pour la plupart des mesures d'enfermement dans des établissements assimilables à des

HP

, il n'y a pas de durée maximale prévue par la loi - en général c'est un an, reconductible à peu près indéfiniment (le principe c'est que la personne y reste jusqu'à ce qu'elle ne représente plus un danger pour la société...)


Il est intéressant de noter que des mesures similaires existaient déjà depuis 2008 pour certains crimes de «

 

droit commun

 

» : meurtre, viol, torture, actes de barbarie, séquestration et enlèvement. Ça concernerait très peu de personnes actuellement, mais on se doute que cette loi va permettre de renflouer les dispositifs existants.


2) Une injonction préfectorale d'examen psychiatrique : de ce qu'on comprend, à n'importe quel moment (pas besoin d'être en gav ou en examen, ou même d'avoir «

 

troublé l'ordre public

 

»), le préfet peut obliger une personne à subir un examen psychiatrique approfondi - par un psychiatre figurant sur une liste établie par la cour d'appel. C'est vraiment sur la base de suspicion de «

 

radicalisation

 

» et de «

 

troubles mentaux

 

». Et bon quand on sait que les fichiers d'Hopsyweb sur les personnes hospitalisées sous contraintes sont croisés avec ceux des «

 

fichiers de traitement des signalements pour la prévention de la radicalisation à caractère terroriste

 

», cela fait déjà une bonne liste de potentiels suspects. Si le certificat médical émis par le psychiatre va dans ce sens, le préfet peut décider d'interner la personne en

HP

 sans son consentement (mais ça, ça existait déjà bien avant). Autant préciser que cette visite au toubib n'est pas facultative : on a la possibilité de faire appel au juge administratif en théorie, mais si on refuse de voir le psychiatre ou si on ne s'y présente pas dans le délai imparti, c'est perquiz, pour se rendre au rendez-vous sous escorte.


3) Une mesure judiciaire de rétention pour les condamnés de droit commun «

 

radicalisés

 

» - là, la loi viserait spécifiquement les gens qui seraient passés par la taule (au moins 10 ans) pour des faits non-liés au terrorisme, mais se seraient «

 

radicalisés

 

» en prison. Là encore, en fin de peine, une commission évalue si le détenu présente une «

 

dangerosité particulière

 

». Si oui, et contrairement à la rétention de sûreté terroriste, la personne n'est pas ré-enfermée, mais elle a droit à l'équivalent d'un suivi

SPIP

 très renforcé, pour veiller à sa «

 

réintégration

 

» : ce suivi peut inclure une obligation de taff ou de formation, un suivi psychiatrique, l'obligation d'habiter dans une zone déterminée... En gros, un contrôle très approfondi de la vie de la personne dans ses moindres aspects.


4) Le renforcement des

MICAS

 (avec notamment moins de possibilités de les contester). Ce sont les «

 

Mesures Individuelles de Contrôle Administratif et de Surveillance

 

», qui incluent déjà la possibilité de …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Tlaib, Democrats Call for Israel to Release Palestinian Doctors From Detention
content:
Israel has killed over 1,700 Palestinian health care workers in three years of genocide in Gaza.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A group of House Democrats has called for Israel to release hundreds of health care workers, including physicians like Hussam Abu Safiya, from detention as Israel’s genocide in Gaza reaches into its fourth year.

Six Democrats, led by Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García (Illinois), released a joint statement on Tuesday condemning Israel for its “systematic persecution” of Palestinian health care workers and demanding their release from arbitrary detention.

“Over the last three years, the Israeli government has systematically destroyed the health system in Palestine, murdering at least 1,700 Palestinian doctors, nurses, paramedics, and other healthcare workers and destroying dozens of hospitals. It has arrested and arbitrarily detained hundreds of Palestinian healthcare workers, including at least 16 physicians who continue to be held in inhumane conditions,” the lawmakers wrote.

The Democrats specifically call for the release of Abu Safiya, who Israel has held in its torture camps for nearly two years, where they have starved and tortured him, his lawyer says. Abu Safiya is a pediatrician who served as the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza when Israel besieged the area.

The world watched in December 2024 as Israel’s ground raid closed in on Kamal Adwan, with Israeli forces eventually ordering the entire facility to be evacuated, setting it ablaze and arresting Abu Safiya. The hospital was left in ruins after Israeli soldiers were done with it.

“Among [those detained] is Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, whom the Israeli government has arbitrarily detained since 2024 and tortured to the point of near-death after previously murdering his son and brutally attacking his hospital,” the lawmakers went on.

The statement was signed by Representatives Pramila Jayapal (Washington), Summer Lee (Pennsylvania), Ilhan Omar (Minnesota), Delia C. Ramirez (Illinois), and Rashida Tlaib (D-Michigan).

Israel's systematic destruction of the Palestinian healthcare system and targeting of healthcare workers is at the heart of its genocide. We must stand up for those targeted for saving lives. Free Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya. Free Dr. Mazen Rantisi. Free Dr. Dima Amin.…

The Democrats also called for an end to arms transfers to Israel and urged Congress to block the Trump administration’s planned $2.8 billion package of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — which is slated to be paid for by U.S. taxpayers. Other Democrats have also vowed to work against that transfer.

In three years of genocide in Gaza, Israel has killed more than 1,700 health care workers and has left zero hospitals fully functioning in the enclave. Israeli forces have also detained more than 400 health care workers from Gaza without charges or a trial in their torture camps.

Israel has killed nearly 600 aid workers since October 7, 2023, according to UN counts.

“Over the past three years, people’s ability to access health care in Gaza has deteriorated dramatically, with medical facilities lying in ruins, hospitals increasingly running out of basic supplies, and patients unable to access essential medicines and treatments. Restrictions on essential supplies such as engine oil and spare parts are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances, and water systems running, with generators breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced,” said Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in a statement on Monday.

“It will take generations to recover from the harm that has already been done over the past three years, and in the preceding decades, while the excruciating consequences of Israel’s ongoing genocide are still being felt every day,” said Amande Bazerolle, the head of MSF’s emergency response in Gaza.

content:

author: Béla
title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.


The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.


About the session


Date & time:


15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 Trans communities and activists 


Register here


What the session will cover 


Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.


The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? What community networks and resources are already available? What might help or hinder efforts to build similar community-led care?

title: Le temps des promesses
content:
Alors que la jeunesse française embrase le pays, nous avons interviewé Christian Ingrao pour son nouveau livre

Le Temps des promesses

. La situation présente est le produit d'une lente glaciation de l'espérance qui avait été annoncée non par des prophètes, mais par des historiens, des économistes, des ingénieurs agronomes, et toutes ces littératures grises qui enregistrent, en même temps qu'elles font, l'espérance et ses vacillements. Nous vivons les derniers moments d'une série de promesses nées aux lendemains de la mutation anthropologique des guerres mondiales, et dont la force d'élan et d'entraînement s'est tarie au tournant des années 1980. En réactivant une méthode matérialiste inspirée de Engels et Marx, Ingrao parvient à reconstruire la « sociogenèse de l'espérance », depuis une multitude d'observatoires, dont le temps présent nous dit la fin.

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.


The root cause


According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.


The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.


“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.


Lives of patients at risk


The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”


The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.


The nurse also told

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.


Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.


It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.


Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Paul Messersmith-Glavin
title: A Lifelong Organizer Shares Lessons on Sustaining Activism for the Long Haul
content:
Organizer Chris Dixon discusses how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Writer and organizer Chris Dixon has his fingers on the pulse of North American grassroots movement. Dixon has extensively and repeatedly traveled throughout North America, talking with people working for social change — engaging with activists concerning their successes and heartbreaks, their frustrations and dreams. His first book, Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements, published in 2014, focused on antiauthoritarian organizers and politics across a range of movements of the 2000s and early 2010s, including migrant justice, prison abolitionism, and Occupy Wall Street. His new book, For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World, focuses on how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Movement elders I am close to — now in their 70s — who maintain radical political commitments developed in their youth, benefitted from both the intense community that formed around movements for Black Power and liberation, the youthful counterculture and the New Left, and anti-war movements, as well as from their own inner convictions that served as an animating passion. For these elders, political engagement is a kind of vocation. Though they continue to maintain relationships with those comrades who are also still alive and committed to political struggle, those vibrant communities they once thrived in are gone. Only their specific commitment to the possibility of freedom and liberation keeps them going.

Coming of age politically in the 1990s, we also had strong bonds of friendship born through relentless organizing meetings, demonstrations, and coalition work. It seemed we could collectively change the world. Thirty years later, only a handful of us remain involved. Why? Why do people stop organizing, beyond and in addition to the realities of acquiring increasing responsibilities as we age? Why do people give up on the possibility of creating fundamental social and structural change together over the long term? How can we cultivate and sustain caring radical communities that support us all, while drawing new people in, or welcoming them back? These are some of the questions Chris Dixon sets out to answer in For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World. The interview that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Paul Messersmith-Glavin: Who should read your book?

Chris Dixon: I wrote For the Long Haul as a practical guide with two main audiences in mind. On the one hand, I wanted to warmly welcome people who have recently become involved in radical political efforts, especially those who have joined movement upsurges since 2020. I’m particularly thinking of the Movement for Black Lives and Palestine solidarity organizing, but also renewed labor militancy and collective defense of queer and trans people. A lot of people I talk to who are newer to movements — many but not all of them younger people — are hungry for conversations about how to sustain lifelong political commitments.

On the other hand, I wanted to speak lovingly to my peers — long-time activists and organizers who have been involved in movements for decades. Many of us talk informally with our friends about the challenges we face in staying actively involved on the left. We’re working a lot to pay our bills, reckoning with disabilities and chronic health conditions, and holding significant care responsibilities for kids, elders, and others in our lives. So many of us are deeply exhausted and hungry for realistic advice about how to stay steady in the fight.

I also wanted to sympathetically address people who participated in movements of the left at one time or another and then moved away from active involvement. I know many people who have followed this trajectory. Rather than being moralistic or dismissive, I wanted to remind them that they’re always welcome back. And I wanted to suggest that perhaps, together, we can build some better structures and practices for helping people stay engaged.

You have spent a tremendous amount of time travelling around the U.S. and Canada, listening to on-the-ground organizers. What have you learned?

title: 'Aile Sağlığı Merkezleri, satılacak bina değil, sağlık merkezidir'
content:
Eylem Nazlıer [email protected]

Türkiye’de koruyucu, birinci basamak sağlık hizmetlerinin yurttaşla buluştuğu en önemli noktalardan biri olan Aile Sağlığı Merkezlerinin (ASM) geleceği, merkezlerin fiziki koşullarından kira giderlerine, deprem güvenliğinden personel eksikliğine kadar risk altında. Kamuya ait binalarda bile kiralarına yüzde 300’e varan zamlar istenen ASM’lerde aile hekimleri zor durumda.

Birlik ve Dayanışma Sendikası Genel Başkanı Dr. Ahmet Mehlepçi, ASM’lerin mümkün olduğunca kamuya ait, depreme dayanıklı ve sağlık hizmetinin gerektirdiği fiziki standartlara uygun binalarda hizmet vermesi gerektiğine vurgu yaparak “ASM’ler yalnızca hekim, ebe ve hemşirelerin görev yaptığı binalar değildi. ASM’ler; koruyucu sağlık hizmetlerinin, gebe, bebek ve çocuk izlemlerinin, bağışıklama hizmetlerinin, kronik hastalık takiplerinin ve vatandaşın sağlık sistemiyle ilk temasının gerçekleştiği temel sağlık kuruluşlarıdır” hatırlatmasını yaptı. Bu nedenle ASM’lerin geleceğine ilişkin kararların yalnızca bina, taşınmaz veya bütçe konusu olarak değerlendirilemeyeceğini dile getiren Mehlepçi, “Konu doğrudan sağlık hizmetine erişim, hizmetin sürekliliği ve kamu yararıdır” diye konuştu.

Sağlık Bakanı Kemal Memişoğlu’nun Kasım 2025’te 1000 yeni ASM yapacaklarını açıklamasından bu yana sadece 278 ASM’nin hizmete girdiğini, 370 ASM’nin inşaatının sürdüğünü ve 352 ASM’nin proje aşamasında olduğu bilgisini veren Mehlepçi, Türkiye genelinde ise yaklaşık 8 bin 300 ASM bulunduğunu söyledi.

Yeni ASM yatırımlarının elbette önemli olduğunu belirten Mehlepçi, mevcut merkezlerin ise kentsel dönüşüm, deprem riski, yüksek kiralar veya taşınmaz satışları nedeniyle hizmet dışı kalmasının önlenmesi gerektiğini vurguladı.

Bir taraftan yeni ASM’ler yapılırken diğer taraftan mevcut merkezlerin kentsel dönüşüm, deprem riski, yüksek kiralar veya taşınmaz satışları nedeniyle hizmet dışı kalma tehlikesiyle karşı karşıya olduğuna dikkati çeken Mehlpeçi “Mart 2026’da TBMM’ye sunulan soru önergesine verilen cevapta İstanbul Kadıköy’deki 33 ASM’den 7’sinin kentsel dönüşüm nedeniyle yıkıldığı ve hizmet veremez hale geldiğini söyledi. Mahlepçi kaç yeni ASM açıldığı kadar, kaç ASM’nin kapandığı, yıkıldığı, tahliye edildiği, taşındığı veya başka bir ASM’nin içine sıkıştırıldığının da kamuoyuyla paylaşılması gerektiğini aktardı.

ASM binalarının deprem güvenliğinin de önemli bir sorun olduğunu belirten Mehlepçi, 2025 yılında yapılan bir çalışmada ASM binalarının yaklaşık üçte birinin 1999 öncesinde inşa edildiğinin ortaya çıktığını söyledi. 6 Şubat 2023 yaşanan depremlerde ortaya çıkan tablonun bu konuda vahim olduğunu hatırlatan Mehlepçi “2026 yılı başında sahadan elde edilen verilere göre Hatay’da 96 ASM konteynerlerde hizmet veriyor. 103 ASM kendi binasında hizmet vermeye devam ediyor ancak bunların bir bölümü deprem güvenliği açısından risk taşıyor. Yaklaşık 56 ASM ise tahliye veya yıkım sürecinde” dedi.

Öte yandan ASM’ler için sorunun yalnızca deprem güvenliğiyle sınırlı olmadığını, ASM’lerdeki sağlık hizmetinin niteliği ve çalışanların koşullarını etkileyen başka fiziki sorunların bulunduğunu da dile getiren Mehlepçi durumu şöyle anlattı: “Penceresi, yeterli mekanik havalandırması bulunmayan kan alma odaları, lavabosu olmayan, iki veya üç sağlık çalışanının aynı odayı kullanmak zorunda kaldığı ASM’ler de var. Hatta bazı çalışma alanları hasta mahremiyetini sağlamaya da elverişli değil.”

Yıkım veya tahliye kararı verilen merkezlerde görev yapan sağlık çalışanlarının başka bir ASM’nin mutfağına, dinlenme odasına veya ortak kullanım alanına yerleştirilerek yeni bir aile hekimliği birimi oluşturulmasının kalıcı bir çözüm olmadığının altını çizen Mehlepçi, “Bir sağlık hizmetinin verilebilmesi için yalnızca bir oda bulunması yeterli değildir. O alanın sağlık hizmetinin niteliğine, çalışan güvenliğine ve hasta mahremiyetine uygun olması gerekir” dedi.

Kamusal sağlık hizmeti sunulan ASM’lerde yükün önemli bir bölümünün aile hekimlerinin üzerine yıkıldığına ve özellikle büyükşehirlerde uygun bina bulmanın giderek zorlaştığına işaret eden Mehlepçi “Kiralar da ASM’lerin sürdürülebilirliğini tehdit eden seviyelere ulaştı. Aylık 100 bin TL ve üzerinde kira ödeyen ASM örnekleri var. Elazığ’da bazı ASM’ler yüzde 350’ye varan kira artış talepleriyle karşılaştı. ASM’ler birer ticarethane değildir. Burada yürütülen faaliyet kamu sağlık hizmetidir” uyarısını yaparak buna rağmen yüksek kira bedellerinin yanı sıra elektrik, su, doğalgaz, temizlik, bakım-onarım …

author: Karin Jervert
title: Mad in the World at the Mad in Norway International Film Festival
content:
A

s a ‘voices and visions gal’, as I call myself, who recently reclaimed her life from psychiatric abuse and over-medication, every little life thing I do is so big and impactful that one of my friends at home has a running joke about me. She texts me after every event, trip, workshop, or talk and asks, “Are you changed?” and my answer is always “Yes!” because returning to life after losing so much to psychiatry has a mind-blowing impact even in the minutia others gloss over. Everyday things that “normal” people ignore, or feel are just living—to me are a miracle of sorts.


This is what I expressed at the restaurant when I toasted a room full of friends and colleagues in the Mad in the World Network who had come to Norway for a Mad in the World meeting and the Mad in Norway International Film Festival. Earlier in the day, a lot of jet-lagged folks sat around a room excitedly talking together about what would be possible in the future. At the restaurant, I spoke of the miracle of the moment we were living in just then, the fact that all of us arrived in person in Lillehammer to meet and to enjoy these films on rethinking mental health.


I looked around that room and saw my heroes. All fighting in their own way for the thriving, health, and sovereignty of people in mental distress around the world. To me, it was an epic gathering, the impact of which we will continue to see ripples of in the coming months.


A few years ago, many of us met in Copenhagen, and the effect was a bit of the same. Our in-person smiles, hugs, laughter, and learning gave us heart in the fight for informed consent and human rights in psychiatry. We inspired each other with our individual and collective efforts. I am always aware of the resistance we face—the derision from psychiatry, the trolls, the personal attacks, and the fear. Every time I am in a room with these people, I see not only our strength and our hearts, but what we are up against. And I know we will keep fighting together on this path. And I am grateful we have each other.


Mad in the World at Mad in Norway International Film Festival, Lillehammer, Norway


And as always, when I arrived home again to the USA, I really was changed. So, I can report back to my friend, that yes, life—and this work—is still a beautiful miracle to me.


The schedule was well-organized, each film well-selected, and the panels after the films were informative. It was a wonderful privilege to encounter in person the directors, thinkers, artists, musicians, members of clinical teams, and parents involved. There was not a moment that one of the 208 attendees was left without something to enjoy, grow in, or experience something new and exciting—let alone the beauty of the town itself.


Even the late-night showings were well-attended. Late one evening, when the credits rolled on The Dance Club, the entire audience got up and danced. Some of my favorite people I spotted smiling and dancing in the aisles, a beautiful sight to see! This film was so beautiful I recommend that you check it out. Grete Johnsen—who, by the way, was a huge part of our everyday, who was always waiting at the welcome desk with a smile (and a few Post-It notes for me to attend to)—has put up links directing to where most of these films can be screened. You can find those here. So, those of you who could not attend can at least enjoy some of the films on various streaming platforms.


There were so many wonderful films it is impossible to mention them all here in this brief review.


As an organizer I am most proud of creating the art show, which you can view here. It was an honor to see the work of many survivors on the big screen. Another wonderful privilege was hosting, with Alan Robinson from Locura en Argentina, the music and poetry show. The musicians and poets showcased at this event brought the night to another magical place filled with powerful expressions of self-empowerment after psychiatric harm. They reminded us of the collective joy art can bring. The highlight was a circle dance, hands clasped, around the entire theater while the Mad in Brasil team—with the musicians from the Creative Humanities Score (another great movie!)—led us in music and singing and dancing together. I saw enormous smiles and childlike joy on so many of my beloved colleagues and friends’ faces. A moment I won’t soon forget.


So as to not go on forever about this amazing event, I’ll now summarize in brief. This festival was a hard-won success …

I den ungsocialistiska pressen hade så tidigt som år 1907 agitation förts för syndikalismen. I majnumret år 1910 av den fackliga tidningen Bageriarbetaren gjorde bagarnas förtroendeman, Anders Sjöstedt, som var redaktör för nämnda tidning, ett försök att hindra syndikalismens spridning bland bagarna, vilka i stort antal gripits av den syndikalistiska agitationen. Då skrev undertecknad ett genmäle mot den mäktiga förbundschefens angrepp under rubriken: **.."Man säger... Genmäle på artikeln i majnumret."*

"Man säger, att bagarna skola vara med då det gäller att upplösa förbunden och bilda Lokala Samorganisationer", inledde vår förtroendeman Anders Sjöstedt, och tillade sedan: "Tack för erbjudandet, men skall man då behandla bagarna på samma sätt som man vill göra nu, tycker vi synd om bagarna." På detta sätt vill jag svara att aggressiva kommer arbetsgivarna alltid att vara oavsett vilken organisationsform arbetarna har, tills dess de får så kraftigt mothugg så de lugnar sina rovdjurskänslor. Och då behövs det sannerligen syndikalistiskt försvarskraft. Därför kan inte en förtroendeman, om än med stor vilja, uträtta något ensamt - utan en vaken, handlingsfull och slagkraftig organisation.

Lusten att krossa arbetarnas organisationer har icke saknats av de privata arbetsgivarna - ej ens från styrelser och föreståndare för kooperativa bagerier i södra Sverge. Närmare angivet Skåne. Där har till och med öppna strider utbrutit.

Alla arbetsgivare vill ha utgifterna så små som möjligt. Men inkomsterna så stora som möjligt. Detta får ju främst arbetarna, producenterna, lida för.

Vidare hade Sjöstedt skrivit: "Lyssna på styrelserna för 'Föreningsbagerierna' och och för en del kooperativa bagerier vilka diskutera om bagarna på ett utmanande sätt, när det gäller deras avtal."

För min del tyckte jag att bagarna icke skulle bry sig om vad dessa konservativa styrelsemedlemmar pladdrar om. Och är det någon underhandling de ej vill bry sig om och önskar de icke vara med om någon överenskommelse som vi vet att de kan gå med på, behöver vi icke kompromissa och springa och berusa dessa herrar i all evighet, och tigga om rätt till mänsklig existens. Vi ha förmåga att slå till! Vi äro de starka! Gör slut på fegheten! Det är vi som är producenter!

Därför behöva att omändra organisationerna till kampduglighet och smidig anpassningsförmåga efter de förhållanden som kan uppstå. Vad de Lokala Samorganisationerna angår så äro de mest praktiska, och kan med heder avlösa de gamla tungrodda byråkratiska fackföreningarna, som äro i majoritet i detta land.

Att inte organisationsfrågan är ett aktuellt spörsmål just nu, bland bagarna, är en lögn av stort mått. Den är aktuell och skall bliva det ännu mer när tiden är mogen. Trots vad Sjöstedt skriver! Och hans ångest som så tydligt märks!

Allt sedan de reformistiska organisationernas början har i regel "förts de korslagda armarnas strid", som de gamla ledana är så förtjusta i - till borgardömets fromma!

Detta har visat sig odugligt. Vi har ju bagerier, som är bojkottade ända sedan den tid som "Svenska Bageri- och Konditoriarbetareförbundet" startades. Och det var inte i går!

Vi har exempel på detta i Göteborg och i Uddevalla, ja lite varstans i detta land.

Det skulle taga allt för stort utrymme i anspråk att räkna upp alla. Och när uppgörelse kommer att träffas vet ingen! Och ingen gör något för att ändring skall ske. Ingen delar ut så mycket som en bojkottslapp för att upplysa allmänheten om förhållandet, att konflikt råder. Därför behövs det pigga organisationer i vilka medlemmarna äro socialistiskt skolade och nyktra. Då kan vi marschera framåt och vinna något, trots det att arbetsgivarna göra allt för att slå ned vår frammarsch. Detta få ingen glömma!

Man skriver så ofta och påstår att folk är så egoistiska, att de ej vill betala avgifterna till föreningarna …
