author: anred
title: Un octubre con convulsión y más bronca
content:
Hoy asistimos al acorralamiento de la Corte Suprema de Justicia por la afrenta contenida en la legitimación de la entrega de la tierra en el mismo acto en el que avasalló derechos de los ex combatientes. Los reclamos contra la cabeza del poder judicial pueden extenderse en los próximos días a todo el arco político-institucional. Por Daniel Campione*


Una corte arrinconada en Neuquén


En los últimos días se han registrado crecientes protestas contra el fallo de la Corte Suprema de Justicia en el que habilitó la venta ilimitada de tierras a extranjeros. La ira se potencia porque lo hizo mediante un argumento procesal y no de fondo. Un modo artero.


Como es sabido, negó legitimación a un centro de excombatientes de Malvinas, el Cecim de La Plata para su intervención en la causa. Y así repuso la vigencia de una ley puesta en cuestión tanto en lo político como en lo judicial.


La primera reacción callejera que registraron los medios fue un “escrache” en un hotel de San Martín de los Andes, localidad turística patagónica. Los tres magistrados integrantes del máximo tribunal estaban allí el 1 de octubre con motivo de un Congreso de Funcionarios de Tribunales Orales Federales.


Variados sindicatos de la zona y organizaciones de izquierda y peronistas cercaron el hotel en el que se alojaban los jueces.


Los ya característicos carteles de fondo blanco y letras desparejas (inspirados en el reivindicatorio de Malvinas durante el mundial) aparecieron allí. Una de las inscripciones fue específica y elocuente: “Corte Suprema vendepatria”. Otra asumía la defensa de la tierra en sus diversos aspectos: “La tierra no se vende, no se quema ni se desaloja”.


Fue en tierras neuquinas, cerca de donde se encuentra el Lago Escondido “encerrado” por Joe Lewis. También próximas a las enormes propiedades del coloso italiano Benetton, que se aproximarían a 1 millón de hectáreas. Y a las comunidades mapuche siempre hostilizadas y amenazadas de desalojo. El reclamo por la tierra adquiere una resonancia especial en toda la región.


Así, el primer día del mes, comenzó lo que despunta como un ciclo de protestas crecientes contra los “supremos”. Las y los comentaristas encontraron enseguida reminiscencias con lo que ocurrió en 2017 después del “2X1” para los genocidas. Los integrantes de la corte de entonces casi no pudieron salir de sus casas. Hasta que se desdijeron de su sentencia pro impunidad dando paso a una sonora victoria popular.


Sin parangones lineales con la trascendencia de la lucha contra la impunidad por los crímenes de lesa humanidad, la soberanía territorial es asimismo una causa popular muy sensible y masiva. Acicateada además en estos meses por el gigantesco eco del mudo pronunciamiento sobre las islas de la selección nacional, vencedora de los británicos.


Los sentimientos populares convergen en la dirección de un enojo en el que se combinan varios elementos pasibles de ir para el mismo lado. Juega un papel importante la bofetada simbólica contra un pronunciamiento tan masivo como cercano en el tiempo.


Nos referimos a la movilización del 6 de agosto pasado. La que condujo al retroceso de la ley mal llamada “de inviolabilidad de la propiedad privada”. A su rescate partió raudo el tribunal. Tal vez sin la mínima ponderación, por el apresuramiento, de las consecuencias factibles de la jugada.


También en Buenos Aires


El martes 6 de octubre se registraron, tan sólo en la capital de la nación, episodios de distinta intensidad y gravitación que refuerzan lo ocurrido el día 1. Es más, insinúan ya una tendencia.


El más acotado, más no irrelevante por el lugar, transcurrió en la Facultad de Derecho de la Universidad de Buenos Aires.


Allí “La Cámpora” y alguna otra agrupación, manifestaron disgusto en el salón de actos de esa facultad. En una “gala” por la entrega de un premio llamado “Quorum”, ingresaron con carteles al auditorio del establecimiento educativo. Estaba prevista la presencia del “cortesano” Rosatti junto con Julián Ercolini, juez federal a cargo de algunas causas contra Cristina Kirchner.


Allí se articuló el reclamo general por las tierras con el de tinte más partidario. La hace tiempo habitual consigna “la patria no se vende”, alusiva en este caso al tema tierras, fue completada con reclamos por la libertad de Cristina Kirchner. Quienes estuvieron en el lugar hacen referencia a un reducido núcleo estudiantil como actor de la protesta.


Resulta nada desdeñable que un ministro del tribunal supremo haya …

author: Novara Media
title: Inside Huawei: the Company That Terrifies the West
content:
Huawei makes the pipes and cables that power the Chinese internet. Its global reach has made China into a superpower.


Huawei is often accused of spying for China. But how was the US so sure that Huawei’s technology could be used for spying? Because they had already hacked it and were using it to spy themselves.


That’s not even the strangest episode in the company’s history. Its installations were bombed by the UK and US in Iraq before 9/11. In 2018, its infrastructure allegedly pinged back the secrets of the Africa Union to China overnight. And it now stands accused of doing business in Iran.


Eva Dou is the author of the deeply researched

House of Huawei: The Secret History of China’s Most Powerful Company

.


She spoke to Richard Hames about the geopolitics of telecommunications, how Huawei made China into a global superpower, and whether or not Huawei is, in fact, a wing of the Chinese state.

author: Amanda Seitz
title: Trump Health Officials Have Been Consulting AI Executives in a Private Chatroom
content:
Tech leaders have been working with the administration to integrate AI into health care and medical record systems.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A cadre of elite techies, financiers, and high-level Trump administration officials have spent a year quietly charting an extraordinary and rapid campaign to persuade Americans to use apps and other artificial intelligence-powered tools to manage their healthcare and medical records.

As that campaign has unfolded, administration officials have granted tech companies an unusual opportunity to nudge the nation’s health department toward a loosely regulated future for AI health apps in which the government reimburses them for services as it does medical professionals.

In February, federal health officials invited those businesses — including tech giants Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, Apple, and Google — to a listening session on conversational AI products for patients, such as chatbots. Representatives from at least 35 industry organizations attended the meeting held by the Food and Drug Administration, which is responsible for regulating health apps as medical devices. Companies were prompted in advance to explain their AI products and how they access patients’ sensitive medical information.

But the meeting did not appear on the FDA’s public calendar or regulatory notices, nor was the public invited. Rather, the invitation for a select group to help shape federal policy governing AI in healthcare was extended in a chat room on the messaging service Slack.

“This is a great opportunity to support HHS’ goals and share your state-of-the-art understanding of safe Conversational AI development and monitoring to help FDA shape future guidance,” CMS senior policy adviser Morgan Taylor wrote in the Slack workspace.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has not formally announced the chat room through federal regulatory channels, though CMS officials have talked about it at industry conferences. Legal experts said the chat room resembles a federal advisory panel, which would be required to operate in public view.

KFF Health News reviewed thousands of Slack messages, meeting transcripts, and video recordings that reveal how the Trump administration has granted the industry a direct line to top government officials — including former head of the Department of Government Efficiency Amy Gleason.

The conversation took place behind the scenes as federal health officials publicly worked to integrate AI and other technology into nearly every aspect of healthcare, a plan they’ve branded the “Health Technology Ecosystem.”

“We wanted to give industry a chance to play in the sandbox of government-supported healthcare,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said in September at the public launch of an initiative that allows health apps to bill Medicare for AI services such as wearable device tracking. Last week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivered an enthusiastic endorsement of AI in healthcare, claiming it is “much better informed than any doctor in the country.”

Meanwhile, HHS staff even promised that a recently launched Medicare App Library would serve as a lucrative pipeline for those businesses to get new users. The library’s webpage currently promotes only two dozen commercial apps to millions of American seniors and those with disabilities.

As Trump officials sell it, Americans will get easier access to their medical records so apps can swiftly provide health or wellness advice. In practice, however, so will the tech companies.

Doctors, meanwhile, are increasingly worried about how patients use and share their medical records with the nascent technology.

“Some of these tools just aren’t ready for primetime,” said John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association. “We don’t have enough data about them. We don’t understand how they work, how they’re using the information. There’s no liability if these tools get things wrong.”

CMS officials declined to answer several questions about the Slack workspace, including about its legality.

“CMS is focused on giving Medicare beneficiaries greater access to their health information and useful digital tools while promoting an open, interoperable healthcare system,” Gleason, now chief product officer for the newly created Office of Health Technology and Products at CMS, wrote in an …

author: Jake Johnson
title: Coalition Files Emergency Petition to Stop Trump FCC’s Media Consolidation Spree
content:
“The FCC simply cannot ignore the laws Congress makes,” said one of the advocates behind the motion.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A coalition of nonprofit groups and labor unions filed an emergency petition on Friday aimed at blocking the Federal Communications Commission’s recent repeal of a decades-old rule that limited consolidation among television broadcasters, a move that would allow media conglomerates to seize even more control over local news stations.

The petition states that the Republican-controlled FCC’s decision — pushed by Chair Brendan Carr and approved in August in a 2-1 vote along party lines — was “plainly contrary to law and violates core administrative law principles.” The filing notes that Congress enacted the rule barring any single TV broadcaster from reaching more than 39% of US households — and only Congress can roll it back.

“The FCC simply cannot ignore the laws Congress makes just because the current agency head wants to,” said Matt Wood, vice president of policy at Free Press, one of the groups that joined the new motion. “Chairman Carr serves only [President] Donald Trump, not the people of this country. Carr threatens broadcasters when their coverage angers the administration, but tosses them bones like this repeal when the biggest broadcast conglomerates toe the line.”

The petition was submitted days after the FCC published the final text of its order repealing the National Television Multiple Ownership Rule, which Carr’s FCC effectively ignored earlier this year when it approved Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of rival TV company Tegna — a deal that Trump vocally supported. Free Press noted that the merger would “give Nexstar access to 80% of US households over the nation’s broadcast airwaves.”

Clayton Weimers, executive director of Reporters Without Borders North America, said Friday that repealing the 39% cap “eliminates the only meaningful limit on TV ownership consolidation in the US, reducing media pluralism, eliminating choices for news consumers, and threatening jobs in an industry already reeling from widespread layoffs and closures.”

“If allowed to move forward, this policy will benefit a small handful of powerful owners of media conglomerates, while harming journalists, local and independent TV stations, and, not least of all, the American people,” said Weimers.

Cable industry groups are also taking action against the FCC over its move to repeal TV ownership constraints. Ars Technica reported earlier this month that “cable lobby groups notified the Federal Communications Commission that they will sue the agency to block its controversial repeal of the National Television Ownership Rule.”

The industry’s filing states that the FCC’s repeal “arbitrarily and capriciously ignores the harms that will surely follow from allowing broadcast station groups to exceed the National Cap, in the form of increased retransmission consent fees for multichannel video programming distributors … and higher monthly TV bills for consumers.”

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

author: Alaa Dmeida
title: I Carry the Key to My Destroyed Home in Gaza to Keep Alive My Dream of Returning
content:
The word “ceasefire” entered the news on October 11, 2025, but it has still not entered our lives as a reality.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

On the night of March 18, 2025, while we were observing Ramadan, my family and I woke to the sound of very loud explosions, one after another.

We all woke up frightened and began asking my father, “What happened? Has the war returned?”

My father did not answer. No one knew anything.

We stayed together, waiting for morning, not knowing what was happening.

We had not expected the first ceasefire to be broken. We had already spent nearly a year living through war, and we had been looking forward to Ramadan with the hope that it would come without the bombing and fear.

The first ceasefire in Gaza had lasted nearly two months before Israel resumed its airstrikes that day, ending the period of relative calm that had begun on January 19, 2025.

Then everything became quiet. We ate suhoor, the early morning meal eaten before the daily fast of Ramadan begins, we prayed Fajr (the pre-dawn prayer), and went back to sleep.

But we were overwhelmed by grief and exhaustion. We loved Ramadan, and we had been waiting for it for a whole year, hoping that it would finally be a time to feel some happiness after a year of displacement, hunger, war, and exhaustion.

I remember thinking that even Ramadan, the holy month that we had hoped to celebrate after everything we had been through, had not granted us even one year of peace.

After the war resumed, we were displaced to a school near our home in Jabalia.

As the months passed, life became more difficult, and hunger began to set in. But we stayed. We held on to our neighborhood and our home. We remained there alongside our relatives and neighbors.

Then Eid al-Adha came. That year, it fell on Friday, June 6. For some reason, I was very excited about Eid. I cannot remember why. We prayed Eid al-Adha, listened to the Eid sermon, wore our nicest clothes, and congratulated one another on the end of Ramadan. But the celebration did not last long.

Friday is the weekly holy day for Muslims, when we gather for Friday prayers after a sermon. When the time for Friday prayers approaches, men would normally begin making their way to mosques or prayer areas.

But suddenly, the bombing began.

The sky above us filled with helicopters dropping bombs, while terrifying artillery shells were fired around the area.

We had decided to stay, but an evacuation order was then issued for the entire area. We were forced to leave, abandoning the school that had been our shelter, our home and our neighborhood in Jabalia.

For days, we hoped we would be able to return. We thought the evacuation might only be temporary, perhaps part of an expansion of the Israeli military operation, and that we would return within a week or two.

Then, on June 11, my father decided to go back toward Jabalia to check on our home. When he came back and told us that it was gone, we were devastated.

Shortly afterward, another evacuation order was issued for the area where we were staying. We left again, this time for the Daraj area of Gaza City.

But the displacement did not end there. As the bombing intensified in Daraj, we were forced to leave again.

On September 22, we arrived at Al-Awda Camp in Al-Zawaida, in central Gaza. The name of the place carried a deep meaning for us. “Al-Awda” simply means returning home — returning to the place where we belong and to the life we had before the war. Despite everything we had been through, we were still holding on to that hope.

The key to our home was still in the bag I had packed when we were first displaced. I carried it with me every time we were forced to leave one place and move to another.

We knew our home had been destroyed, but that did not erase our desire to return. We did not know what that return would look like or what we would find when we got there. We simply wanted to reach the place that had once been our home and see with our own eyes what remained.

The key to our home was still in the bag I had packed when we were first displaced. I carried it with me every time we were forced to leave one place and move to another. I never used it, but I never left it behind either.

I knew it could no longer open the door I remembered because the door itself was no longer there. Still, I kept carrying it.

author: Joedy McCreary
title: Outside Groups Have Spent Nearly $2 Billion on Campaigns This Election Cycle
content:
The top 6 groups had spent more than $60 million each as of October 5.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Outside groups have poured nearly $2 billion into this election cycle with weeks of spending still to come, and a small cluster of groups is responsible for a growing share of that money.

The top six outside groups — the Senate Leadership Fund, Texas PAC, No Going Back PAC, WinSenate PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund and Americans for Prosperity Action — spent more than $60 million apiece as of Oct. 5, according to federal disclosure reports analyzed by OpenSecrets.

Together, they accounted for more than $678 million — or more than a third of the outside spending by 794 groups tracked by OpenSecrets, and a sum nearly equal to the combined spending of the next 34 groups. Just 16 organizations account for more than half of all outside spending during the current cycle.

Each of those groups serves a distinct purpose. For example, the Senate Leadership Fund works to elect Republicans to the Senate while the Congressional Leadership Fund does the same for the GOP’s House candidates and WinSenate PAC supports Democrats running for Senate seats. Texas PAC is a new SLF-linked organization created to back Ken Paxton, that state’s Republican Senate nominee. Americans for Prosperity Action is among the organizations backed by conservative billionaire Charles Koch. Another new group — the President Donald Trump-linked and MAGA Inc.-funded No Going Back PAC — spends to oppose Democrats in battleground races.

The money they’re pouring into races is becoming even more concentrated. As recently as Sept. 21, the top six groups accounted for 28% of all spending and 20 of them made up nearly half of all outside spending. That concentration still falls short of 2022, when the top six outside groups accounted for 45% of all outside spending tracked through that year’s election.

That concentration of spending isn’t new, California State University, Chico political science professor Diana Dwyre said.

“There are big spenders, and there aren’t that many of them, and I think that’s been a trend since” the advent of super PACs, Dwyre told OpenSecrets.

The modern outside spending landscape traces its roots to the Supreme Court’s decision in Citizens United v. FEC. That 2010 ruling opened the door for corporations, unions, nonprofits and PACs to spend unlimited amounts on elections as long as that spending remains independent of the campaigns they support. That, combined with a separate lawsuit against the FEC, paved the way for super PACs.

Sixteen years later, super PACs remain the dominant outside-spending vehicle. Formally known as independent expenditure-only committees, they account for the vast majority of outside spending — more than $1.5 billion of it. Four of the top six spenders are super PACs. The others — Americans for Prosperity Action and CLF — are hybrid committees. Also known as Carey committees, they can make both unlimited independent expenditures and capped direct contributions to candidates. Overall, hybrid committees account for nearly $406 million.

Conservative groups continue to dominate the spending landscape, pouring in more than $1.1 billion compared with nearly $727 million for liberal organizations. Another $120 million in spending was not tied to either side. Six of the top seven spenders were conservative, led by the Senate Leadership Fund, which has spent nearly $174 million.

Many of the biggest names are familiar: Three of the top four from the 2022 midterms are back near the top of the list this year under the same names, topped by the Senate Leadership Fund, which also led the way in 2022. Two are hybrid committees supporting the parties’ House candidates: The Congressional Leadership Fund, which spent $227 million four years ago, has spent $67.2 million so far in 2026 to rank fifth — four spots ahead of the Democrats’ House Majority PAC, which spent $145 million in 2022 and $49.3 million this year.

The exception is SLF’s Democratic counterpart — WinSenate PAC — which was registered in 2024 and is run by Senate Majority PAC. WinSenate ranks fourth with nearly $109 million in spending. Senate Majority PAC itself ranked third in 2022.

“All they care about is their team winning,” Dwyre said of the party-aligned super PACs. “And that’s a more pure goal. … They’re still political animals, but at least their motives are easy to …

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Shawn Fain’s Victory in United Auto Workers Elections Keeps Union on New Course
content:
The election was a referendum on the union’s new direction, pursuing bold contract fights and new organizing campaigns.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain has won a second four-year term, with an overwhelming lead in member balloting for the union’s top officers.

The election was a referendum on the new fighting direction Fain has taken the union by leading 2023’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, other bold contract fights, and new organizing campaigns.

It marks the second time members have voted for their top officers in the union’s 91 years. UAW members voted to switch to a one-member-one-vote system in December 2021.

With votes in eight of the union’s nine regions counted as of Friday morning, Fain had more than two-thirds of the vote, against five opponents. His nearest competitor, incumbent vice president Rich Boyer, had 14 percent.

Fain is running as part of the United UAW slate. His slate-mate for secretary-treasurer, Brandon Campbell, has also garnered two-thirds, against two rivals including incumbent Margaret Mock.

The slate’s candidates for the three vice president spots appeared on track to be elected with 19-25 percent each in a field of 11 candidates. (VP candidates need 16.7 percent to win.) The slate has also won all the regional director races counted thus far that it contested.

If the slate sweeps, as appears likely, it will hold all the seats on the union’s International Executive Board except for one regional director.

Fain has won a majority of the vote in most locals, from assembly plants to legal services, and a plurality in almost all the rest. Boyer, who heads the union’s Stellantis division, has won just two of the union’s dozens of big locals: Local 140, Warren Truck, his home local, and Local 1700 at Sterling Heights Assembly Plant, both near Detroit.

Turnout was low and similar to the 2022 election, with a little over 10 percent of the union’s 400,000 active members and 600,000 retirees returning their mail ballots. (Retirees also vote on top officers in the UAW.)

While some expected Fain’s strongest support to come from the higher education and legal aid locals on the East Coast, turnout there was down by more than half from 2022, with fewer than 2,000 ballots counted. Turnout was up in Local 4811 at the University of California, which went 75 percent for Fain, but still only 2,500 of 60,000 members there voted. As in the last election, it was members in the big manufacturing locals that were key to Fain’s victory.

Perennially online candidate Brian Keller had 7 percent of the presidential vote. As the ballots were counted he took to Facebook Live to swear at members for 30 minutes and call them “morons” for not voting for him.

In phone interviews with a dozen members, auto workers cited pensions and post-retirement health care as their key motivators for backing Fain. They also raised concerns about tackling automation and job security.

But the biggest issue was the better contracts the UAW has won since Fain took office.

Infighting between Fain and his opponents on the outgoing International Executive Board—Rich Boyer, Margaret Mock, and Mike Booth—came up, but people drew widely different conclusions, with many repeating the phrase Fain “isn’t perfect.” Jeep worker Megan Fagan in Toledo said some members have checked out due to the internal drama, reinforcing the cynical view that not much has changed.

For most, though, disagreements at headquarters were not of interest or on their radar. They looked at their pay stubs and voted accordingly.

Boyer, Mock, and Booth came together to form the Integrity Slate but failed to offer a counter to Fain’s focus on fighting the companies and launching new organizing drives. Boyer’s main pitches in his campaign statement in the UAW magazine were to lower union dues and reduce the staff at union headquarters.

“Fain and his slate are the only ones that have a real program for the future of the union,” said historian Nelson Lichtenstein, author of Walter Reuther: The Most Dangerous Man in Detroit. “You’d think the other people would have come up with something aside from they want to reduce dues, which means basically cripple the new organizing.”

“The members chose Fain, despite the Monitor’s best efforts to create turbulence, because we’re ready to fight for retirement health care and protection from …

title: US-weit erster Streik bei den Amazon-Liefer- und Zustellerdiensten in Kalifornien/Palmdale – weitet sich aus

Dossier

Dafür marschierten sie unter anderem am 24. April 2023 vor die Amazon-Konzerzentrale in Palmdale. Obwohl es diesen Vertrag nun gibt, weigert sich Amazon, ihn zu befolgten und zahlt weiterhin niedrige Löhne und tut nichts für bessere Arbeitsbedingungen. Am 15. Juni 2023 haben die Amazon Zustellfahrer*innen und Versandmitarbeitenden in Palmdale/Kalifornien deshalb zum ersten Mal gestreikt. author: CMI Argentina
title: AySA: una venta demasiado barata y un entramado de vínculos con el poder libertario
content:
La operación acumula cuestionamientos judiciales y contables, pero hay algo más detrás del consorcio que se quedará con la empresa de agua potable: Filiberti, los Neuss y US$ 30 millones que no aparecen.


Por Gladys Stagno


La privatización de AySA se da entre fuertes cuestionamientos de todo tipo: un precio muy por debajo del valor de mercado, una cautelar vigente que la impediría, y US$ 30 millones que no aparecen. Pero lo más turbio del negocio tiene que ver con sus nuevos dueños.


Vayamos por partes.


Precio vil


Como lo anunció allá por julio del año pasado, el Gobierno encabezado por Javier Milei avanzó con el proceso de privatizar el 90% del capital accionario de Agua y Saneamientos Argentinos (AySA), que actualmente se encuentra en manos del Estado, por los próximos 30 años.


Y encontró un comprador: el consorcio conformado por

Rowing, Arcos, Transclor y PHX presentó la mejor oferta por US$ 340,2 millones

, bastante por encima de los US$ 285 millones que ofreció el Grupo Roggio, pero

US$ 110 millones por debajo de lo que había calculado el Ministerio de Economía

.


Riesgo inminente


Pero la licitación se llevó adelante sin precio base, lo que permitiría vender las acciones incluso a este monto. Y también a pesar de que continúa vigente una cautelar en primera instancia confirmada por la Cámara en lo Contencioso Administrativo de La Plata, que había sido promovida por el defensor del Pueblo bonaerense, Guido Lorenzino.


Lorenzino advirtió un “riesgo inminente” de que la privatización de Aysa derivara en un deterioro del servicio y en

 el abandono de trabajos planificados.

 El Tribunal coincidió “en aras de tutelar el compromiso ambiental y la salud de la población”, aunque también resolvió girar la causa al fuero federal, para que ésta resuelva la cuestión de fondo.


¿Cuánto vale Aysa?


Por otra parte, la Auditoría General de la Nación (AGN) alertó sobre que la subvaluación sería aún mayor. El hallazgo del organismo pone la lupa sobre el proyecto “Financiamiento Adicional para el Proyecto de Desarrollo Sustentable de la Cuenca Matanza-Riachuelo”, que preveía una inversión de US$ 1.350 millones financiada con un préstamo del Banco Mundial.


Pero

el Tesoro nacional adelantó US$ 30 millones (unos $42.935 millones)

, que no fueron reembolsados ni registrados en los estados contables, y que representarían casi el 10% de la oferta del grupo inversor ganador. En la práctica implicarían

una subvaluación del 66,57% de las inversiones realizadas por AySA

.


Los nuevos dueños


Las sospechas sobre el apuro por vender a un precio subvaluado una empresa superavitaria —que en 2025 obtuvo ganancias por $22.000 millones— se agravan si se hace zoom sobre los nombres involucrados en el principal oferente.


Se trata de

un grupo liderado por Mauricio Filiberti, dueño de Transclor y conocido como “El rey del cloro”

, proveedor de AySA del insumo que utiliza para potabilizar el agua desde 2009. Su principal socio es

Rowing S.A., constructora presidida por Walter Román, quien a través de otras empresas de su holding aportó $40 millones a la campaña de La Libertad Avanza en 2025

, según advirtió el defensor del Pueblo adjunto de la provincia de Buenos Aires,

Walter Martello

.


Martello también denunció que —según información del Ente Regulador de Agua y Saneamiento (ERAS)— el holding ganador de la licitación de AySA facturará US$ 93 millones extra por año por un cambio de zonificación. “En 4 años tendrán recursos que pagarán los usuarios equivalentes al valor de la empresa”, planteó. Y agregó que ese dato “es central y debería conocerse antes de la firma del contrato”.


Por otro lado, señaló que Filiberti también es socio en el control de Edenor, lo que genera otro conflicto de intereses. “AySA es el mayor consumidor de electricidad del AMBA y, por lo tanto, el principal cliente de esa distribuidora. De confirmarse la adjudicación, un mismo grupo quedaría a ambos lados de esa relación comercial”, alertó.


Además, Filiberti no estaría solo. Según reveló

La Política Online,

 detrás del empresario “aparecen camuflados los hermanos Juan y Patricio Neuss, los empresarios favoritos del gobierno libertario”.


Los Neuss y Santi Caputo


Los hermanos Juan y Patricio Neuss vienen ampliando su presencia en áreas estratégicas de la economía. En los últimos meses participaron de adquisiciones y concesiones vinculadas al negocio energético y quedaron asociados al proceso de privatización de activos clave …

author: Randi Beers
title: An early Inuit relocation scheme – Part 2
content:
On July 13, 1878, the

Florence

 was finally free of ice and left its winter harbour.


That same day Capt. George Tyson encountered a party of Inuit travelling by boat in the sound, off on a caribou hunting trip.


From them he learned that the other Inuit who had promised to accompany him had changed their minds and already gone inland hunting caribou. He prevailed on some of the newcomers to join his venture, but they declined.


Three days later, Tyson put in at the American whaling station at Kekerten to pick up skins.


He noted, “We were employed today preparing a place in the vessel’s hold for the Esquimaux to live during the passage to Greenland.”


There he took one more man, three women and two children. Was one of these women a wife for Alokee?


With these additions, the complement of Inuit was 15, five each of men, women and children.


“And I think that will be enough,” noted Tyson.


There were also 30 dogs and a number of sleds aboard.


They crossed the sound to Blacklead Island where “I took a boat and an Esquimaux crew and went on shore to allow the Esquimaux to have a talk with their friends and relatives. We bade them good-by and returned to the

Florence

. Set sail at 4 p.m.”


On Aug. 5

 they were off Godhavn, Greenland, where Tyson put his dogs ashore on an outer island.


The governor was absent, but had left orders with his subordinates that there should be no communication between vessel and shore.


Tyson wrote, “I asked the reason for this strange order, and was informed that one Capt. Adams of the Scotch steamer

Arctic

 had been here in the early spring and told the governor that the Esquimaux and crew of the schooner

Florence

 were all diseased.” 


Henry W. Howgate conceived of the relocation scheme. (Photo courtesy of Wikipedia)


That situation had not changed by Sunday, Aug. 11

, when Tyson, with his Inuit friends still aboard, wrote, “It is

Sunday, and the little bell on shore summoned the people to church. We have no communication with them. Every day the boats from shore, containing the half-breeds of the settlement, come around the schooner to gaze upon the West Land Esquimaux, but none of these visitors are allowed on board.”


The following day, Tyson had more details on the reasons why he and his Inuit were not allowed ashore: “Mr. Smith, the inspector, sent a boat… with a request for me to come on shore, as he wished to see me. He says that the surgeon and captain of the steamer

Arctic

 informed him that there was a great deal of sickness among the Esquimaux in the gulf, and that it was only to protect his own Esquimaux from disease that he issued the order forbidding communication with us.” 


The governor told Tyson that he had read in a Danish newspaper that Howgate’s planned expedition to Ellesmere Island had been postponed, but urged Tyson to wait until the arrival of the next Danish ship in case it carried instructions for him.


By Aug. 22

 a Danish vessel had arrived but it brought no news for Tyson. He had run short of supplies and had already purchased 1.5 tons of coal, 18 kilograms of sugar, 18 kilograms of coffee and 11 kilograms of tobacco. Now he bought another half ton of coal, 125 kilograms of bread, 18 kilograms each of sugar and coffee, and another 11 kilograms of tobacco.


With no news from the United States, Tyson, disappointed, left Greenland. He had been ashore, as had the two scientists, but it appears that the only Greenland soil the Westland Inuit set foot on was the island where the dogs had been disembarked, and to which the Inuit went periodically to tend to them.


There is no indication that they met any Greenlanders except those who came out to the ship by qajaq but who were not allowed onboard. They may have communicated verbally over the side of the ship.


The weather was unpleasant for most of the Davis Strait crossing. It was with relief that Tyson reached Naujartalik Harbour on Aug. 31. The scientist Ludwig Kumlien noted that they enjoyed a few days of rest there, “rest from the howling of the wind and wave and from the far less musical squall of the juvenile Eskimo and the fiendish howls of the dogs.”


On Sept. 2

, Tyson formally discharged the Inuit, noting, “I gave them one boat, four guns, all the remaining ammunition, two opera-glasses, one suit of clothing each, nearly all of the Danish bread we bought at Disco, some little molasses, and one tent.”


He took on water for the homeward voyage, but bad weather …

author: Jack Dura
title: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe Files New Lawsuit to Shut Down Dakota Access Pipeline
content:
Ten years after the Standing Rock protests captured national attention, the tribe is still fighting the project.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe on Friday filed a new lawsuit to try to shut down the Dakota Access oil pipeline, continuing a decadelong battle over the project.

The tribe filed the case in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration and three federal officials of those agencies. The lawsuit seeks to overturn the Army Corps’ May record of decision granting an easement for the pipeline’s river crossing upstream of the tribe’s reservation, among other actions.

“For ten years, Standing Rock’s concerns about this pipeline have not changed, and for ten years we have fought to protect our water, our Treaty rights, and our people,” Standing Rock Sioux Tribal Chairman Steve Sitting Bear said in a statement. “The Army Corps has now chosen to move forward without addressing those concerns. Until this pipeline is shut down, we will continue to defend what generations before us protected for our children.”

In 2016 and 2017, thousands of people gathered near the project’s Missouri River crossing to demonstrate against the pipeline, which the tribe views as a threat to its water supply from a potential rupture.

In 2020, a federal judge ordered a more rigorous environmental review of the pipeline’s river crossing. In May, the Army Corps issued its record of decision granting the crucial easement for the pipeline, which has continuously operated since mid-2017.

The tribe said the final environmental impact statement issued by the Army Corps in December 2025 does not resolve issues surrounding the safety of the pipeline, spill response, threats to the tribe’s sole source for drinking water, treaty rights and the federal government’s obligations to the tribe.

The tribe also expressed concerns about the pipeline potentially increasing capacity to 1.1 million barrels of oil per day which the tribe said would change operational risks related to spill volume and emergency shutdown, according to court papers.

“We should not have to live with unanswered questions about the safety of our water,” Sitting Bear said.

The pipeline transports an average of 500,000 to 525,000 barrels of oil per day from North Dakota’s Bakken oil field to Illinois. The environmental review considered a capacity of up to 1.1 million barrels per day. The pipeline’s operational capacity is 750,000 barrels per day, North Dakota Pipeline Authority Director Justin Kringstad said.

The federal pipeline safety agency declined to comment on the lawsuit. Officials with the Army Corps and pipeline developer Energy Transfer did not return emails seeking comment Friday.

State and industry officials have said the pipeline is safe and needed infrastructure for transporting oil from North Dakota, the No. 3 oil-producing state in the U.S. Energy Transfer has said the pipeline is among the safest in the world, complies with regulations and crosses at least 95 feet below the riverbed.

The tribe argues a spill would threaten the health and welfare of the Standing Rock community. The lawsuit also seeks to rescind the federal pipeline safety agency’s approvals of spill response plans, and block the transport of oil through the river section until spill response plans meet federal law, according to court documents.

“The Tribe files this action to require the defendant agencies to respect the Treaty rights and sovereignty of the Tribe and to protect the waters of the Missouri River and the ancestors resting at the water’s edge,” the tribe said in court papers.

In 2024, Standing Rock filed a federal lawsuit against the Army Corps over its ongoing environmental review. In 2025, a judge dismissed the case. The tribe appealed, but dropped its appeal earlier this year.

Other court cases still linger in connection with the protests, including Energy Transfer’s lawsuit against several Greenpeace organizations and a Dutch lawsuit brought by Greenpeace International against the pipeline developer.

author: Corey Larocque
title: Minority government outcome stalls PQ referendum pledge
content:
It’s hard to believe Nunavik is a hotbed of Quebec separatist sentiment, but there you have it.


The region’s newly elected member of the Quebec national assembly is Sonia Caron, of the separatist Parti Québécois that won a minority government in Monday’s provincial election.


Fortunately, the PQ’s failure to form a majority government means it will be much harder for the its leaders to deliver on their key promise to hold a referendum on Quebec’s future within Canada during its first term.


Just two days after the election, Caron was cagey about talking about a referendum.


“I can’t comment on that at this point,” she said in an

interview

 with Nunatsiaq News on Wednesday.


Nunavik is better off in a united Canada, so it should come as a relief the PQ’s ability to hold a sovereignty referendum will be tempered.


On the campaign trail, party Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said a PQ government would hold a referendum on separating from Canada in its first term. But there’s one condition — the referendum would only be held after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office. Presumably, that would put any vote off until 2029, when Trump’s second term ends.


Having lost two referendums — in 1980 and 1995 — many PQ supporters are reluctant to hold a third referendum if it looks like they will lose again. A lot of Parti Québécois supporters only want to hold a referendum if there are winning conditions.


It’s hard to imagine that the winning conditions will exist by 2029. Will Quebecers be more inclined to look for independence after four years of a trade war with the U.S.? Will national unity be galvanized because Canadians have stood together to respond to the Trump-imposed economic challenges?


The PQ’s election as a minority government (it won 59 of the national assembly’s 127 seats) likely dampens St-Pierre Plamondon’s ability to deliver on his pledge to hold a referendum. The federalist Liberal and Conservative parties won 40 and 19 seats, respectively, leaving the Québec solidaire’s with the balance of power.


National unity is facing another — more immediate — challenge in the form of a referendum taking place in Alberta on Oct. 19.


Albertans will go to the polls to answer a question about whether the provincial government should hold a binding referendum about whether the province should remain in Canada.


If there’s a silver lining in the election of a separatist party in Quebec, it could be that the Ungava riding’s representative will be sitting in the government benches.


It’s similar to the idea that Nunavut MP Lori Idlout is better able to get the federal government’s attention on northern issues by sitting as a Liberal than she could while sitting in the House of Commons as a New Democrat.


Over the past eight years, Ungava’s MNA was Denis Lamothe, who was also a member of the Coalition Avenir Québec government. The Coalition party paid attention to the massive northern Quebec riding. Ministers like Ian Lafrenière, who held the Indigenous affairs and public security portfolios, visited the riding from time to time.


Northern Quebec was on the Coalition Avenir Québec’s radar.


Hopefully, that will continue as Caron takes over as the riding’s new representative in a new PQ government.

author: Dalia Abu Ramadan
title: A Shadow of Fear Hangs Over Gazans Amid Israeli Defense Minister’s Threats
content:
Israel Katz says Israel will forcibly displace 1 million Gazans if “even one Israeli soldier” is abducted.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

We are about to close out three years and enter another since Israel invaded Gaza, but we are not leaving the war behind to begin a new life. We are entering yet another year without knowing when this war will end — or whether it will end at all.

The fear remains. The destruction remains. The threats remain. It feels as though each passing year does not bring us closer to an end, but closer to the possibility of another war.

Despite everything we are living through in Gaza, we understand what it means to live one day at a time — to hold on to every simple moment we can still have. Imagine planning for another morning, perhaps for the simplest of things: going out with the friends you still have, or taking your family to the sea in the morning, amid all this destruction, simply to experience a moment that feels like life.

Then, as you are planning that ordinary morning, you hear a statement from Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, who said on September 22: “If even one Israeli soldier or civilian is abducted, the city of Gaza — with its homes and terrorist towers — will be evacuated southward of its one million residents.”

Words like these are enough not only to disrupt your day, but to shake your entire future. The first question we asked ourselves was: Where would we go? Is there anywhere left for us to go?

“Everyone is talking about how the possibility of an Israeli soldier being captured has become impossible, that it will not happen, and that it could be an excuse to provoke people in Gaza and pave the way for the war to return,” Haneen Salem, a photographer in Gaza City, told me. “I am certain something will happen. No one knows what, but there is a shadow of fear hanging over Gaza’s civilians.”

Even my father said, “Expect it to happen at any moment,” warning that we could be forcibly displaced yet again, especially because we are living through another difficult period in Gaza. The intensity of Israeli bombardment had increased in the weeks leading up to Katz’s statement, and warplanes had not stopped flying overhead at night.

Words like these are enough not only to disrupt your day, but to shake your entire future. The first question we asked ourselves was: Where would we go? Is there anywhere left for us to go?

We are being asked to imagine another war while we are still living inside the aftermath of the one that was supposed to have ended.

The so-called ceasefire took effect at noon local time on October 10, 2025. A year has passed since that announcement, but the war has not ended. It is true that the intensity of the escalation and displacement has eased compared to the height of Israel’s war, but the bombardment and destruction have continued. So, what does it mean to hear threats of the war returning with the same ferocity when we have not even begun to recover from what has already happened?

When the “ceasefire” was announced, I believed the war would end as the wars of 2021, 2014, and previous years had ended — with a clear conclusion, a moment when we would know that the war was truly over. I expected that, immediately after the announcement, we would begin clearing the rubble, rebuilding what had been destroyed and slowly putting our lives back together.

Instead, it felt as though the war continued in another form, behind the scenes — a reality visible only to the people of Gaza who have been living through its consequences every day. Today, we still have not recovered. Even the most basic medical necessities remain unavailable, the siege is tightening, and the consequences of the war continue to surround every part of our lives.

The collapse of the Al-Sadah building in Tal al-Hawa is one example of what this unfinished recovery looks like. The building had been home to approximately 80 displaced Palestinians. In the early hours of September 16, it collapsed, with parts of the structure also falling onto nearby buildings and tents that were sheltering other displaced families. Rescue teams initially estimated that around 100 people, including at least 50 children, were trapped beneath the rubble. After rescue operations ended, Civil Defense teams confirmed that 21 people had been killed, including 12 children and five women, while 45 injured people were taken to …

title: Thwarted in Courts, Trump DOJ Increases Pressure on States to Obtain Voter Rolls
content:
The administration is pursuing numerous strategies to manipulate data, neutralize safeguards, and disenfranchise voters.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The upcoming midterm elections seem destined to serve as a bellwether for the state of democracy in this deeply fraught period of U.S. electoral history. The results will be interpreted as a referendum on the catastrophically unpopular second Trump administration and will determine much of the legislative landscape over the next two years. Substantial Democratic victories could significantly constrain Trump’s powers or even place his presidency in jeopardy, and the Election Day performance of crucial structures and procedures could attest to either a resilient democracy — insofar as the country’s very flawed but still-vital electoral institutions are worthy of the name — or, conversely, a system that has at last been compromised by years of right-wing attacks, leaving the integrity and legitimacy of future votes in serious question.

The Trump administration, keenly aware of the stakes, has gone to unprecedented lengths to exert undue influence on electoral procedures. Having mobilized the Department of Justice (DOJ), the FBI, and other arms of the federal government now radically subservient to Trump, the administration is pursuing numerous strategies, legal and extralegal, to bludgeon its way into sensitive databases, neutralize electoral safeguards, and disenfranchise legitimate voters, with the intent of negating the wishes of the U.S. public and illicitly enshrining their own power.

In reality, states are fully capable of maintaining their own rolls without the DOJ’s intervention (removing individuals who have died or moved out of state, for instance). And, more to the point, cases of “illegal voting” are extraordinary rarities, and have collectively had less-than-negligible — zero — impact on any real election results. Since the DOJ’s rationales are utterly fictitious, it’s not hard to imagine that there may be other motives underlying their aggressive nationwide efforts to access voter rolls, given that these initiatives originate from an administration led by and filled with election deniers.

Obtaining unredacted state rolls has not always been a simple matter, and the Trump Justice Department has in many cases resorted to strongarming, undermining, or otherwise attempting to manipulate state governments and other agencies to further its aims. Any plan to wrest election operations away from the states must inevitably find ways to circumvent the fundamental obstacle to federal control — Article 1, Section 4 of the Constitution, according to which elections are to be overseen solely by the states. Of course, questions of constitutionality have never burdened Trump’s conscience, and he has openly announced his desire to “nationalize” elections and place them under federal (i.e., his) jurisdiction. Were that to someday occur, unfettered voter roll access would be a boon for election manipulators.

Still — in court, at least — the Trump administration’s efforts to attain that level of nationwide control have been less than fruitful. The Trump DOJ has initiated numerous lawsuits that seek to force states to sign data-handover agreements: no fewer than 31 to date, with one of those filed against Washington, D.C., and the rest against states, most of them governed by Democrats. title: Mother tongue, identity and collective memory
content:
The mother tongue is more than the first language through which a person begins to discover the world. It is a bridge through which identity takes shape, a sense of belonging is established and collective memory is passed down through generations. From the language in which a child begins their education to the language in which a person can express themselves when receiving healthcare, the mother tongue encompasses far more than a purely cultural debate. Restricting the use of a language, excluding it from education or denying it a place in public life undoubtedly affects an individual's relationship with themselves and society.


People first learn to make sense of the world through the relationships around them. Alongside family and social relationships, language becomes part of this initial process of understanding. Sometimes, the first word a person learns is more than a means of communication; it becomes part of their connection to their family, their past and the community to which they belong.


Psychologist Siyabend Aslan defines the mother tongue as “the first home into which a person is born when they open their eyes to the world.” Aslan spoke to ANF about the place of language in human life, saying, “Rather than simply being an ordinary tool for communicating with the outside world, it lies at the very heart of our identity, our past and our sense of belonging.”


Identity and collective memory


The mother tongue is one of the foundations on which identity is formed. Much of a person's connection to family, society, culture and the past is carried through language. Restricting the use of a language can therefore also affect a person's relationship with the community to which they feel they belong.


Aslan explained the impact of restricting a community's use of its mother tongue on individual and collective psychological well-being: “Restricting a community's use of its own mother tongue is tantamount to telling its members directly, ‘You, your ancestors and your feelings are worthless.’”


Aslan described the psychological impact of this as “linguistic trauma,” adding: “It is a profound wound that causes people to feel ashamed of their own roots and to experience a deep sense of worthlessness.”


Alienation from one's roots


Researcher and linguist Zana Farqînî placed the issue within a broader social context. Farqînî said, “Assimilation is not merely about banning a language or excluding it from everyday life, education and the public sphere,” and explaining that distancing different communities from their own roots is also part of this process.


Farqînî drew attention to the relationship between language and identity, saying, “Assimilated individuals tend to assimilate into the dominant identity imposed through the dominant language and, over time, begin to feel that they belong to that identity.”


Collective memory, in turn, gives identity its social dimension. Farqînî explained this relationship: “Language is not merely a means of communication. It is the creator, carrier and transmitter of a culture. It is the raw material of all verbal arts and forms of expression. It is the memory of society.”


In short, the weakening of a language affects both the possibilities for communication today and the ways in which the past is passed on.


Passing memory down through generations


The continuity of collective memory depends on the transmission of language between generations. A language known by older family members but difficult for children to understand or speak can gradually disappear from everyday family life. As children become a generation that hears the language but does not use it, passing it on to the next generation becomes even more difficult.


This situation is also clearly evident in the case of Kurdish. Farqînî said, “Today, Kurdish is being lost between generations. The proportion of children and young people who speak Kurdish is quite low, and this proportion is declining with each passing day.”


Farqînî said language use also varies according to age and education level: “Kurdish is spoken more frequently among older and middle-aged Kurds and those with lower levels of education. As education levels rise and age decreases, we see the opposite trend.”


The ability to pass a language on to the next generation is just as important as knowing it. Farqînî said, “A language that is not passed on to children has no future and is condemned to die,” and stressing the importance of using …

title: PYD calls for unity and restraint amid tensions in Hesekê
content:
The Democratic Union Party (PYD) issued a written statement about the provocations in Hesekê. The statement noted that Syria is going through a sensitive transitional period and called on all political and social forces to engage in dialogue, show solidarity and work to build trust.


The PYD stressed that the rise in hate speech and provocations in the region threatens internal peace, emphasising the need to clarify the circumstances surrounding the incidents and hold those responsible to account.


Syria needs a democratic and pluralistic system


The statement noted that Syria is passing through a sensitive and important transitional period. It said that all political and social forces must fulfil their national and historical responsibilities, strengthen dialogue among all of Syria’s communities and work to build trust.


The statement also stressed that steps had recently been taken to make progress on implementing the 29 January Agreement. It said these steps would contribute to strengthening stability, unifying efforts and building a democratic Syria.


‘Hate speech and provocations threaten internal peace’


The statement drew attention to recent security incidents and tensions in the region. It said the developments began with the death of a member of the Foca officers’ unit in Qamişlo, followed by an attack on a vehicle belonging to the security forces, the killing of Sîpan Hiznî, and incidents in Kobanê and other areas.


The statement said that hate speech and provocations on digital platforms had increased alongside these developments. It noted that this situation threatens internal peace, fuels tensions and creates conditions for divisions within society.


The PYD said it was following developments with concern and stressed the need to approach the incidents responsibly and calmly, avoiding hasty reactions.


‘The constitutional rights of Kurds must not be defended’


The statement said that escalating tension between Syria’s communities not only threatens internal peace and the social fabric, but could also be exploited to return Syria to a centralised, uniform system.


It stated that such efforts could be aimed at obstructing the constitutional rights and legal protections of the Kurdish people, preventing all communities, particularly Kurds, from participating meaningfully in building the new Syria, and undermining the gains made under the stated objective of establishing state authority and legitimacy.


The statement emphasised that any attempt to impose exclusion and domination would result in losses for all Syrians. It added that such efforts would also undermine the stability and coexistence that are intended to be established.


Call to identify and hold those responsible to account


The PYD called on the public not to be influenced by hate speech. The statement urged all administrative and security institutions within the Hesekê Governorate, as well as the relevant parties, to fulfil their responsibilities.


It said action must be taken to uncover the truth about the incidents and hold those responsible to account. It also called for measures to protect the public and maintain security and stability.


The PYD further called on political, social and media circles to help defuse the situation, reject provocations and put the public interest first.


‘Preserving coexistence is a shared responsibility’


The statement stressed that preserving internal peace and coexistence among the region’s communities is a shared responsibility. It said that common sense, solidarity and dialogue are essential to achieving this.


It concluded by stating that efforts must be made to build a democratic and pluralistic Syria that respects the rights of all its citizens and guarantees their meaningful participation, enabling them to live with dignity and equality.

title: Memorial in Argentina for Martyr Lêgerîn Çiya
content:
A meeting was held on Friday at

Espacio de Alina

, in the mountains near Córdoba in Argentina. The space was established to keep the memory of Martyr Lêgerîn Çiya (Alina Sánchez) alive and strengthen solidarity among women.


The meeting was attended by feminist groups, indigenous women and comrades from the Kurdish women’s movement. Participants discussed political developments in Abya Yala and the dangers posed by the spread of fascism.


 


Through her struggle and resistance, Martyr Legerin Ciya succeeded in building bridges between Abya Yala, where she grew up, and the Kurdish movement she chose to join, said participants, adding that "she serves as an example and a guide not only within the Kurdish liberation movement but also within many feminist movements in Latin America, particularly in Argentina. The Alina Space, built in the mountains near the city of Córdoba in her memory, aims to become one of the physical places where this connection is forged. Various feminist and women’s collectives participated in the construction—including the physical building—of this space, using natural and traditional materials and methods."


Participants developed a shared analysis of the situation in Abya Yala and the dangers posed by the spread of fascism, and they shared methods of struggle. Together, they participated in rituals that combined the ancestral spirituality of the indigenous peoples represented by the women present with a struggle for survival in the face of the extractivist and capitalist system.


Patrizia, Legerin Ciya’s mother, also attended the event.


Claudia Corol, a feminist activist, popular educator, and journalist, remembered Legerin Ciya with these words: “We want to honor our comrade and sister Alina Sanchez, to whom this space is dedicated. Born in southern Argentina, in Patagonia, she came here, near Córdoba, with her mother Patricia, and as a child she used to run and play in these places.


She then decided to study medicine in Cuba and learned about the struggle in Kurdistan. She was a determined person who did what she loved and desired. She also helped us in the field of popular education to understand what health truly means."


Corol continued: "In Kurdistan, she was helping to establish a healthcare system amid a war with many wounded. We discussed about this by comparing various systems, to understand how to build a healthcare system in Abya Yala, given the military attacks we are currently experiencing. When she returned to Kurdistan, she fell as a martyr: on the one hand, our hearts were broken; on the other, we told ourselves, 'We must continue her struggle.'


In this context, her mother, Patricia, during a meeting of the network of popular educators, proposed that we build this space for popular education and community health right here, in the backyard of the house where she lives. We didn’t know how to do it, yet here we are, doing it. For us, it’s a commitment to remember her at all times, along with the work we’re carrying out in this space—work that has never stopped."


Corol explained that "the goal is for this to become a space for political, feminist, and health education—a place where we can take care of our sisters and comrades and carry on the struggle. Several comrades from the Kurdistan women’s movement have come here, leaving their mark as we built these walls together. We want to make the women’s revolution—which is so important to us—present here as well. I’d like to conclude by sharing an anecdote.


When Alina went to the mountains of Kurdistan, the first thing she said was, 'I have to offer you some criticism!' 'What criticism?' the comrades asked. 'The criticism is,' Alina replied, 'that you, as a revolutionary women’s movement, know very little about the revolutionary women of Abya Yala. But I also have to offer some self-criticism,' she continued, 'and that is that we, as women of Abya Yala, know very little about the women’s movement in Kurdistan and the struggle it is waging. That is why we are here today building bridges, as best we can; and that is why Alina is the pillar of these bridges,' she said."

title: Lawyer Çimen: Public power used to cover up Gülistan Doku case
content:
New developments have emerged in recent months in the investigation into the disappearance of Munzur University student Gülistan Doku, who went missing in Dersim on 5 January 2020. Numerous suspects have been detained or arrested as part of the investigation, while new digital records, witness statements and evidence have been added to the case file.


The number of people arrested in the investigation reached 38 in September, but questions surrounding Gülistan Doku's disappearance remain unanswered, and her family's pursuit of justice continues.


Ali Çimen, one of the lawyers representing Gülistan Doku's family, spoke to ANF about the latest developments in the investigation.


‘The case was systematically covered up’


Lawyer Ali Çimen said six waves of operations had been carried out in the Gülistan Doku case, with legal action taken against approximately 78 people and 38 arrested.


Çimen said the investigation had been ongoing for nearly seven years and that organised efforts had been made to cover up the case from the outset. He explained that they had faced serious difficulties in obtaining certain evidence, particularly because digital data had been deleted over time.


Çimen described the problems surrounding digital evidence and said: “Six waves of operations have been carried out in the Gülistan Doku case. So far, legal action has been taken against nearly 78 people, and 38 people have been arrested. Of course, since this is an investigation that has been ongoing for seven years, and one that has been systematically covered up, we face difficulties in obtaining certain evidence, particularly because data has been deleted.


For example, footage from the City Security Management System (KGYS) is deleted after three months, while records from the Licence Plate Recognition System (PTS) are deleted after two years. Requests have therefore been sent to the central servers to determine whether these records can be recovered. These are the kinds of difficulties we face. The most significant missing element in our case is that we have still not found Gülistan. However, I believe that the Erzurum and Tunceli Chief Public Prosecutors' Offices will eventually return Gülistan to her family as a result of the investigation.”


‘They tried to cover it up, but the truth came to light’


Çimen stressed that the investigation should not be limited to the existing suspects and said: “The case must be investigated from different angles. We expect another operation involving the seizure of assets. We also expect the investigation to be expanded. As you know, the provincial police chief was suspended from duty, although he appeared to be outside the scope of the investigation. We expect investigative proceedings concerning him to continue and expand.


Even after all the years that have passed since Gülistan disappeared, her family has not even been granted the right to mourn.


I believe Gülistan's body will be found. The Erzurum and Tunceli governor's offices will return her body to her family. They failed to protect Gülistan, failed to protect her life, and now they are not even returning her body. Her family is being denied the right to mourn. An organised cover-up was carried out for six years.”


‘Tuncay Sonel’s phone is like a crime machine’


Ali Çimen said an organised cover-up had been carried out in the Gülistan Doku case for six years, with public authority used as an instrument in the process.


Çimen concluded: “The phone of Tuncay Sonel, who was the governor of Tunceli at the time, must be examined as part of the investigation. Tuncay Sonel's phone is like a crime machine. More information will emerge. I do not believe these matters constitute state secrets. Details relating to the crimes must be shared with the public. There are very serious allegations. The necessary investigation must be carried out. The investigation into Tuncay Sonel must also examine the assets involved. Those assets should be handed over to the public.”

title: Internationalist youth delegation applies to meet Öcalan
content:
Members of the Diplomacy Commission of the Youth Assembly of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), together with an internationalist youth delegation from eight countries, submitted an application to the Ministry of Justice to meet with Abdullah Öcalan. The delegation made a statement at DEM Party headquarters following the application, expressing support for the Peace and Democratic Society Process and stressing the importance of Öcalan's freedom.


The delegation included representatives of Contre-Attaque & Autonomie from Switzerland, Sindacato Unione Democrazia Dignità Cobas from Italy, the Prosfygika Squatted Houses Community on Alexandras Avenue from Greece, La Saó from Catalonia, Mala Zêrîn from Austria, Jeunesse Internationaliste Française from France, Cumann Saol Saor from Ireland, and the Democratic Youth Union (YUNA) from Germany.


The statement was read in English by YUNA member Isabelle Marie Whittenberg and in Turkish by DEM Party Youth Assembly member Jiyan Bahadır.


‘The Peace and Democratic Society Process is a historic opportunity’


Isabelle Marie Whittenberg said the delegation had come from European countries to support the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She said Abdullah Öcalan had been targeted by an international conspiracy 27 years ago and had been held on Imrali Island ever since.


Whittenberg said the peace and democracy process was launched in February 2025 following a proposal by Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement. She stressed that the process represented an important opportunity not only for the Kurdish and Turkish peoples but also for all peoples around the world who seek to live in peace, autonomy and with the right to self-determination.


‘Our struggle is shared’


Isabelle Marie Whittenberg drew attention to the importance of international solidarity in the development of societies and social movements, stressing the need to unite struggles in different countries around common goals.


Whittenberg said local struggles shared feminist, anti-capitalist, anti-imperialist, anti-fascist and anti-racist foundations, adding that internationalists had a responsibility to connect these struggles and unite them on a confederal basis. She said the struggle to live in peace and dignity was a common struggle for all humanity.


‘Women’s freedom and solidarity will lead the way’


Isabelle Marie Whittenberg said a free society is founded on democratic values such as communal life, equality, ecology and solidarity, stressing that these values can only be put into practice through organised struggle based on women’s freedom and democracy.


Whittenberg said state and capital domination sought to suppress peoples’ efforts to organise themselves and govern their own affairs. She added that international women’s solidarity would play a leading role in building peace and a democratic communal society.


‘Resolving the Kurdish question will pave the way for the democratisation of the Middle East’


Isabelle Marie Whittenberg drew attention to the historical responsibility of European states for the partition of Kurdistan and the denial of the Kurdish people, saying that internationalists from Europe regarded solidarity with the Kurdish and Turkish peoples as their responsibility.


Whittenberg said a political solution to the Kurdish question that includes the freedom of the Kurdish people would pave the way for the democratisation of the Middle East and, subsequently, the world. She expressed solidarity with the Kurdish Freedom Movement.


‘We demand Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom’


Isabelle Marie Whittenberg called for Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom to ensure the continuation of the peace process, drawing attention to his political position within Kurdish society and its collective consciousness.


Whittenberg said Öcalan had developed theoretical and practical approaches to a political solution to the Kurdish question in recent years, despite harsh prison conditions. She stressed that his freedom was necessary for the continued progress and lasting success of the peace process.


Whittenberg said, “It is impossible to imprison hope, but it is possible to open the cell doors that restrict the creativity and goodwill needed for society to learn to live in peace.”


Call for Abdullah Öcalan’s release

title: Xerîb Hiso: Attempts are being made to provoke conflict between Kurds and Arabs in Hesekê
content:
As steps are being taken to implement the agreement signed on January 29 between the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria and the Syrian Interim Government, security incidents and provocations continue in the region. The incidents began with the killing of a member of the Internal Security Forces in Qamishlo and continued with an attack on a vehicle of security forces, the killing of Sîpan Hiznî, and developments in various areas, particularly Kobanê.


Most recently, groups gathered in the Xiwêran neighborhood of Hesekê and marched toward Kurdish neighborhoods and engaged in provocations. One member of the Internal Security Forces and three civilians were injured in the ensuing incidents.


PYD co-chair Xerîb Hiso spoke to ANF about the provocation in Hesekê.


'The racist mentality that denies the Kurds is active on the ground'


Recalling the January 29 Agreement signed between the Autonomous Administration and the Syrian Interim Government, which came to power in Damascus following the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, Hiso said: “Significant progress is being made on the integration of the security, defense and autonomous administration institutions. Although there are obstacles, these provocations can be overcome when the focus is on dialogue, a common solution and genuine partnership. However, these provocations are spreading with each passing day. This racist mentality that previously denied the Kurds is now active on the ground. They want to attack, and they do not want integration to move forward. They do not want dialogue. They constantly seek to target us through conspiracies and provocations and to undermine the January 29 Agreement and the integration process.”


‘They want to provoke a war between Kurds and Arabs’


Hiso stated that certain groups were organizing these provocations through digital media and encouraging groups from other areas to gather in Hesekê, saying: “They want to provoke major unrest in Hesekê. They want to drag the Kurds into a conflict and provoke a war between Kurds and Arabs. They are trying to undermine relations between Kurds and Arabs. They want to destroy the will to coexist. But Kurds and Arabs are stronger than these provocations.”


‘Provocations pose a risk of conflict’


Stating that the provocations are spreading across an increasingly wider area, Hiso said that similar attempts have taken place in different neighborhoods of Hesekê. Pointing out that attacks on Kurdish symbols and rhetoric of revenge were heightening the danger, Hiso warned that the incidents could escalate into conflict.


The PYD co-chair noted that the Interim Government had yet to issue a statement and criticized those who described the actions as “peaceful demonstrations.” He said: “Those who view these as peaceful actions are actually destroying peace. If the government has a genuine position on this, it must hold those responsible accountable. Those who support these provocations are also complicit in the crime.”


‘ISIS could exploit the situation’


Hiso stated that the communities in the Cizîr region had taken a strong stance against the provocations and recalled that one member of the Internal Security Forces and three civilians were injured in the incidents. Noting that the Interior Ministry had yet to issue a statement, Hiso warned: “Racist and religious extremist incidents must be prevented. The US withdrawal has also reopened the way for ISIS. ISIS is present here as well, and it will exploit this as an opportunity.”


‘The Kurdish people do not want war’


Hiso stated that the situation in Hesekê had calmed down and that the population was remaining vigilant in order to defend the city. He stressed that the Kurds have the right to legitimate self-defense but do not want to be drawn into a war.


The PYD co-chair pointed out that the groups behind the provocations had been brought in from Shaddadi, Deir ez-Zor and Til Berak, and said that the Syrian national flag was being used as a pretext. Stating that the real objective was to deny the Kurds’ language, identity, symbols and will, he said: “The Kurdish people want peace, dialogue, coexistence and domestic peace. But others are trying to provoke conflict and discord.”


Finally, Hiso called on Kurds in Hesekê, across Rojava and in other regions to remain vigilant and not fall for the provocations of racist groups. Stating that the Kurdish people have the right to defend their existence, language, geography …
